items.title: GoldBod must be more accountable to Ghanaians – Haruna Iddrisu
items.description: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has called for stronger accountability at the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), citing the scale of funds involved in its operations and the need to address reported losses. He said attention should focus on improving the institution’s performance and ensuring that its operations, as well as those of the Bank of Ghana, do not generate avoidable losses. “You see, today, you ought to have improved the Gold Board legislation in a manner that it can become more accountable to the Ghanaian people, because the amount of money involved is huge,” he said. Mr Iddrisu acknowledged reports of losses and urged a collective response to the concerns. “So we have a gold board today. There have been reported cases of losses. Let’s not run,” he said. He questioned whether GoldBod and the Bank of Ghana could operate without occasioning such losses, adding: “And I’m saying that is what we must seek to respond to as a country.” The Tamale South MP also criticised the opposition’s decision to walk out of Parliament during the passage of the GoldBod bill. He argued that remaining in the chamber would have provided an opportunity to strengthen accountability provisions in the legislation. “And remember, even when the Goldbod bill was passed, they walked out of Parliament,” he said, describing the action as “Immaturity on their part.” Asked whether he would support changes to the current system to prevent future losses, Mr Iddrisu responded positively. “Why not? President Mahama will accommodate any objective suggestion from any Ghanaian who thinks that this is the way to improve the Goldbod performance.” While calling for improvements, he also defended the economic contribution of the government’s gold interventions, saying they had helped strengthen Ghana’s gold reserves and supported the currency. He maintained that a more stable exchange rate helped businesses plan and reduced pressures on the cost of doing business.

items.title: 200 people at town hall meeting — Wike mocks Amaechi over 2027 prediction
items.description: The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has mocked Rotimi Amaechi over his prediction about the outcome of the 2027 presidential election, claiming that fewer than 200 people attended the former Rivers State governor’s town hall meeting in Cross River State. Wike spoke during his media chat on Tuesday while responding to a suggestion that the emerging opposition ticket involving former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Amaechi was causing concern among supporters of President Bola Tinubu. Recounting Amaechi’s remarks at the meeting, Wike said the former governor had argued that Atiku was positioned to win the election because of the regional distribution of the major presidential contenders. “I watched Amaechi, he had a town hall meeting in Cross River. I can tell you the numbers not up to 200 people,” Wike said. According to the FCT minister, Amaechi told attendees that the election had already been won and explained his reasoning by referring to the candidates’ regions of origin. “He said, ‘Atiku is from where? North. Tinubu is from where? South. Obi is from where? South. Donald Duke is from where? South. Atiku has won the election,’” Wike recounted. He questioned why a vice-presidential candidate would make such a prediction while addressing supporters at a town hall meeting. “How can a vice-presidential candidate go to a town hall meeting, standing and telling his supporters, ‘Do you know how this election has been won?’” he asked. When asked whether Amaechi’s argument was based on the assumption that Atiku, as the leading northern candidate, would have an advantage over his southern rivals, Wike pointed to the outcome of the 2023 presidential election. “In 2023, Atiku ran, Obi ran, Tinubu ran, who won?” he asked. Wike added that the next presidential election would not necessarily follow the same pattern as the previous poll. “I’ve always told you people, 2027 will be totally different from 2023,” he said. items.description: On the advice of the prime minister, President Asif Ali Zardari has approved ex-Pakistan leaves and issued no-objection certificates (NOC) for the chief justices of the Supreme Court (SC) and the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) to make upcoming foreign visits. In a press release issued late on Monday, the Presidency said that President Zardari has approved the trips of Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi and FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan. CJP Afridi would visit the “United Kingdom, South Korea and Japan from Oct 14 to 21 and from Oct 27 to Nov 4”, the Presidency said. Justice Aminuddin would visit Azerbaijan from Oct 19 to 22 to attend TÜRK-AY – a conference of constitutional courts and bodies exercising constitutional jurisdiction in the Turkic world. The FCC was admitted as an observer to TÜRK-AY in July this year, about four years after the forum was established. The president is the competent authority to grant leave to the SC and FCC chief justices under Rule 14 of the 1997 and 2025 orders regarding leave, pension and privileges for the respective court. Under the same rules, the chief justice of each court is the competent authority to grant or refuse leave, or to revoke or curtail leave already granted to other judges of their court. In April 2025, CJP Afridi headed a delegation to the 20th Con­­ference of Chief Jus­ti­ces of the Supreme Courts of Shanghai Cooperation Organisation member states in Hangzhou, China. In June this year, Justice Aminuddin represented Pakistan at the 14th St. Petersburg International Legal Forum in Russia.

items.title: Pakistan, EU agree to boost cooperation against illegal migration
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner on Tuesday agreed to enhance cooperation in border security, legal migration and border management. The understanding was reached during a meeting between the two in Islamabad, which was followed by delegation-level talks. Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s measures against illegal migration, describing the 64 per cent reduction in illegal migration to Europe resulting from the country’s efforts as commendable. He said the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) had demonstrated professional competence despite limited resources, which was commendable. He added that the decline in illegal migration would pave the way for legal migration. Naqvi said Pakistan had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards illegal migration. “After a 64 per cent reduction in illegal migration, our next target is its complete elimination,” the interior minister said, describing illegal migration as a serious global issue. The two sides also discussed the promotion of legal migration and enhancing opportunities for skilled workforce between Pakistan and the European Union. Both sides agreed to further strengthen cooperation in immigration, institutional coordination and border management, and to work together on the EU’s Eastern Corridor Initiative to eliminate illegal migration. They also discussed increasing mutual cooperation to enhance the capacity of Pakistan Coast Guards and agreed to increase collaboration to promote border security and legal migration. Brunner assured Pakistan of all possible cooperation in this regard. The meeting was attended by the interior secretary, special and additional interior secretaries, FIA director general, Federal Constabulary inspector general, NCCIA director general, passports director general, Islamabad chief commissioner and other officials. Last month, Naqvi said Pakistan had recorded a 64pc reduction in illegal migration to Europe, describing the achievement as challenging despite limited resources. He said Pakistan’s next target was to eliminate illegal migration completely, stressing the need to expand legal migration opportunities, adopt modern technology and strengthen institutional capacity. In February, Pakistan and three European countries, Italy, Spain and Greece, reached a consensus on promoting legal pathways to “effectively combat illegal migration”. The three countries endorsed Naqvi’s proposal to establish legal pathways as a strategy to combat illegal migration and human smuggling during a conference.

items.title: Affi Agbenyo’s EC appointment is constitutionally appropriate, but politically, people have the right to remind us – Haruna Iddrisu
items.description: Tamale South Member of Parliament, Haruna Iddrisu, has stated that President John Mahama’s appointment of Emelia Affi Agbenyo as one of the two new Deputy Chairpersons of the Electoral Commission is “constitutionally appropriate”, although critics reserve the right to remind the NDC government of its actions in the past against similar appointments. Mr Iddrisu made this comment on the Joy Super Morning Show on Tuesday, October 13. The swearing-in of 43-year-old Emelia Affi Agbenyo has stoked controversy following her affiliation with the incumbent National Democratic Congress (NDC). The young international development cooperation professional is on record as having served as a spokesperson for the NDC on governance in the 2024 general elections. Since her appointment, social media has been awash with some posts she made in the past that were deemed political in support of the NDC. A video of her speaking on a media platform as a representative of the NDC has also gone viral. As a result, many have questioned her independence and neutrality in such a sensitive office. For many of the critics, the NDC has acted hypocritically, considering it criticised the then New Patriotic Party administration for similar appointments. But Mr Iddrisu says while the criticisms are legitimate, the appointment is equally legitimate. “I know Affi very well, and I’ve worked with Affi. Affi, as at yesterday, was working under my Ministry, under TVET Services as Deputy to the Chief Executive. Now, is it constitutionally appropriate? Those are the questions you should ask. Does the President have the power under Article 45 to appoint? Now, one of the things we have not been able to do well is to use legislation to define the parameters of who is eligible. Beyond Article 45, 46, providing that there shall be an Electoral Commission, which shall have two deputies, we must have legislation which then defines a threshold as to who can enter into the Electoral Commission.” Asked what kind of Electoral Commission he expects, Mr Iddrisu said, “I just want an Electoral Commission that does not endanger democratic ethos and values. Persons who are independent, persons who are courageous, and persons who uphold the values of transparency. “I share this crude idea with you: anytime people get worried about appointments to the Electoral Commission, you know I’ve supervised the Electoral Commission, even as its Chairman and Vice-Chairman, in terms of their budget for seven years. I’m sure I can say that probably maybe Kyei Mensa-Bonsu, I’ll come next in terms of depth and information on the Electoral Commission and its operation within the annals of Parliament. The MP and Minister of Education hinted that there would be major reforms to the constitution to address complex issues such as this. “Now, there’s a school of thought, and I’m sure it’s part of the constitutional review process that President Mahama has ignited, and be assured that there will be political and economic reforms led by President Mahama. There will be far-reaching changes; I’m sure when Parliament comes back, the Attorney General, on behalf of President Mahama, will introduce two important bills in Parliament. One, a bill seeking to amend the entrenched provisions of the Constitution, and two, a bill seeking to amend the non-entrenched provisions of the Constitution.” “So, I think that the appointment is constitutionally appropriate, but politically, people have the right to remind us that if you seek equity, do equity. Maybe that’s what it is reminding us of.” When he was reminded that Affi Agbenyo had publicly campaigned on platforms for the NDC in the past, Mr Iddrisu said it will only be a problem if she does that while in her current position. “If she does that whilst in office, that would be unacceptable as Deputy Electoral Commissioner.” The experienced politician also disputed the notion that EC officials have the power to manipulate results in anyone’s favour. “I was going to share my crude view with you, even though I’m hesitant. In Tamale South, the Electoral Commission, Deputy Electoral Commission- how do they impact my election? It is to provide me with a fair, open, transparent platform. But the onus of winning the election is mine. It’s not that of the Electoral Commission. And the onus of avoiding fraud, or being cheated, or somebody treating you unfairly, is largely also mine. You know, many times, MPs abandon their role. You can check throughout history. Every day, up to the election, I spend my maximum time at the Electoral Commission. I’ll monitor every ballot box, what goes into the box, against the population of that polling station and others, into the night deployment of election officers. “But I can understand the reservations that are being legitimately expressed by the Ghanaian people. If they are unhappy about it, the government has taken note of it,” he stated.

items.title: Why APC included opposition figures like me in campaign council — Wike
items.description: By Ayobami Okerinde The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has explained why the All Progressives Congress (APC) included politicians who are not members of the party in President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 presidential campaign council. Wike, a member of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), said the decision was based on the need to accommodate people outside the APC who were willing to contribute to Tinubu’s re-election bid. He spoke on Tuesday during a media parley in Abuja while reacting to his appointment alongside Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke and Anambra State Governor Chukwuma Soludo as state campaign coordinators in the APC’s revised presidential campaign council. “My thinking is that the president, in his wisdom, said there are those who are not members of our political parties but have something to offer to his re-election, and it’s proper to accommodate them,” he said. He added that the campaign should bring together people willing to support Tinubu’s continuation in office, regardless of their party affiliations. “We have said that the re-election of Mr President should not just be APC, because here is a platform; the constitution does not say an individual can run, you must have a platform, and that platform is APC, which is an umbrella that people will want to use to further their political ambition,” Wike said. “That gives the holistic view that there are those who are ready for Mr President to be re-elected to continue the good work we think he’s doing for Nigeria, and we’re happy to be part of it.” Under the expanded campaign council arrangement, Wike will coordinate the APC campaign in Rivers State and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). Soludo, a member of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), will oversee Anambra State, while Adeleke, who was re-elected as Osun governor under the Accord Party, will coordinate efforts in Osun State. items.title: Rentrée scolaire à Kaolack: Le CEM Moustapha Ndiaye toujours sous les eaux
items.description: La rentrée scolaire démarre difficilement dans certains établissements du département de Kaolack. Au CEM Moustapha Ndiaye, les inondations retardent encore la reprise des cours. Envahi par les eaux et les mauvaises herbes, le CEM Moustapha Ndiaye n’est pas encore en mesure d’accueillir élèves et enseignants. En visite dans plusieurs établissements, hier, à l’occasion de la rentrée officielle des classes, l’adjoint au gouverneur chargé du développement, Mouhamadou Habib Kamara, a constaté une situation globalement satisfaisante, notamment à SOS Bongré, à l’école Sidy Lamine Sow, au lycée technique El Hadj Ibrahima Niasse et au lycée Valdiodio Ndiaye. » Ce premier jour de rentrée est satisfaisant », a-t-il déclaré, tout en reconnaissant les difficultés rencontrées dans certains établissements. Le CEM Moustapha Ndiaye reste toutefois un cas préoccupant. » Des mesures sont prises et les sapeurs-pompiers sont sur le terrain pour soulager », a indiqué M. Kamara, précisant que la situation a été signalée aux autorités centrales. En l’absence de nouvelles pluies, une reprise des cours est envisagée d’ici à la fin de la semaine. Au-delà des inondations, le département fait face à d’autres défis. Selon l’Inspection d’académie, 64 établissements nécessitent une réhabilitation et les besoins en tables-bancs sont estimés à 9 500 unités. Le déficit en personnel enseignant atteint, quant à lui, 354 enseignants dans les cycles élémentaire et secondaire. Mamadou THIAM (Correspondant)

items.title: 95.838 pensionnaires mobilisés autour des valeurs citoyennes
items.description: Le Dahiratoul Moustarchidina Wal Moustarchidaty (Dmwm) a clôturé, le 10 octobre 2026, à Tivaouane, l’édition 2026 de ses camps de vacances dénommés « Re-Création ». Organisée autour de l’éducation spirituelle, de la discipline et de la citoyenneté, cette édition a mobilisé 95.838 pensionnaires dans 670 daaras au Sénégal et à l’étranger. Former des jeunes ancrés dans les valeurs spirituelles, disciplinés et engagés au service de la collectivité. C’est l’ambition affichée par le Dahiratoul Moustarchidina Wal Moustarchidaty à travers ses camps de vacances « Re-Création ». L’édition 2026 qui a pris fin, samedi dernier, à Tivaouane, a enregistré des résultats satisfaisants pour les organisateurs. « Au terme de 21 jours d’activités éducatives, spirituelles et citoyennes, cette édition a réuni 95.838 pensionnaires, dont 11.542 sympathisants, répartis dans 670 daaras à travers tout le Sénégal », indique un communiqué du mouvement. Placée sous l’égide de Serigne Moustapha Sy Al Maktoum et conduite sous la direction de Serigne Cheikh Ahmed Tidiane Sy Capitaine, le camp « Re-Création 2026 » s’est tenu du 7 au 27 septembre autour du thème : « Dund Rammonte », porté par le slogan « N’est-il pas temps d’y associer les cœurs ? ». « Ce thème fait écho à une réflexion de Serigne Cheikh Ahmed Tidiane Sy Al Maktoum : « Dans l’acte de dévotion, n’est-il pas temps d’y associer les cœurs ? ». Il invite à replacer la conscience, la sincérité et l’engagement personnel au cœur de la transmission des valeurs, précise le document. Ainsi, durant 21 jours, les pensionnaires ont été formés autour de la spiritualité, de la discipline et de la citoyenneté. Au-delà de l’apprentissage religieux et moral, le programme a mis l’accent sur le respect, le vivre-ensemble et la responsabilité collective. Et sur le terrain, cette démarche s’est traduite par des actions concrètes. Nettoyage d’écoles, d’hôpitaux et d’espaces publics, réfection de tables-bancs, de portes et de fenêtres, construction de box d’hygiène et distribution de fournitures scolaires ont rythmé les activités. La mobilisation s’est étendue à la Gambie, à la Mauritanie et à l’Europe. « Au total, 538 plants ont été mis en terre à travers le pays (…). Des denrées alimentaires ont été offertes à des daaras, des exemplaires du Coran et des vêtements ont été distribués, et 16 ventilateurs ont été remis à la Maison d’arrêt et de correction de Vélingara », renseigne le communiqué. Souleymane WANE

items.title: Alioune Sall prône une résilience transformatrice
items.description: Lors de l’ouverture du 4e colloque international du Centre des Hautes Études de la défense et de la sécurité (Cheds), la semaine dernière, le professeur Alioune Sall, vice-président de la Commission du droit international de l’Onu, a préconisé une résilience transformatrice, s’attaquant aux causes profondes des vulnérabilités en Afrique. Vice-Président de la Commission du droit international de l’Organisation des Nations unies (Onu) et ancien juge à la Cour de justice de la Cedeao, le professeur Alioune Sall a animé la conférence introductive du 4e colloque international du Cheds, la semaine dernière. Lequel colloque avait pour thème : « Repenser la résilience en Afrique : sécurité, gouvernance et développement durable ». Dans son intervention, l’universitaire estime que l’Afrique doit maîtriser les facteurs de vulnérabilité et prévenir les crises plutôt que d'être condamnée à les subir. À ses yeux, faire de la capacité d'endurance des populations, le principal amortisseur des défaillances de l'État revient à valider et légitimer ces manquements institutionnels. « La survie ne peut pas constituer un projet politique ni une politique publique », a déclaré M. Sall, plaidant ainsi pour la résilience transformatrice qui, d’après lui, relève « d'une médecine préventive et prophylactique », s'attaquant aux causes structurelles des vulnérabilités pour permettre au continent de maîtriser son propre destin. Pour agir concrètement et faire advenir cette résilience transformatrice, il propose trois leviers essentiels : la sécurité, la gouvernance et le développement durable. S’agissant de la sécurité, l’universitaire rappelle que certaines fonctions régaliennes de l’État ne sauraient être remises en cause. La lutte contre le terrorisme, la protection des frontières, et la sécurisation des populations et de leurs biens relèvent de la dimension militaire et des missions fondamentales de l’État. Cependant, précise-t-il, une approche exclusivement militaire de la sécurité révèle très vite ses limites. Pour lui, la sécurité doit dépasser la dimension purement matérielle ou militaire pour devenir une sécurité humaine. « La sécurité multidimensionnelle est à la fois juridique, environnementale, alimentaire et économique. Le concept de sécurité humaine répond à la nécessité d'élargir et d'assouplir une conception trop exclusivement militaire de la sécurité », a expliqué le professeur Alioune Sall. Avant d’ajouter : « Quand l'administration est absente, quand la justice est inaccessible ou quand les citoyens ne connaissent de l'État que ses forces de coercition, l'ordre qui est instauré est un ordre nécessairement fragile ». Sa conviction est qu'un État ne se consolide pas seulement en se rendant redoutable. « Il se consolide en étant présent, juste et utile », dit-il. Confiance des citoyens S’agissant de la gouvernance, Prof Sall a indiqué que la stabilité et la continuité institutionnelle ne sauraient suffire pour apprécier la qualité d'une gouvernance. D’après lui, une gouvernance favorable à la résilience transformatrice doit reposer sur la confiance des citoyens dans les institutions publiques. Il reste persuadé qu' »une élection sans crédibilité, une justice perçue comme dépendante, une corruption impunie ou des territoires abandonnés affaiblissent les États ». « La confiance publique est une infrastructure stratégique, au même titre que les routes ou les ponts. La qualité de la gouvernance doit dépasser la seule question des élections. La démocratie ne peut pas s'épuiser dans l'élection ; l'élection n'est pas l'alpha et l'oméga de la démocratie », a-t-il fait savoir, soulignant que l’Afrique a besoin d’une démocratie continue fondée sur la confiance dans des institutions représentatives et redevables. « L'absence de confiance débilite le corps social, la démocratie, l'État et la société », a regretté le conférencier. Concernant le développement durable, il rappelle qu’il renvoie à la nécessité de protéger l'environnement, de sauvegarder les biens communs et les richesses naturelles, de ne pas les surexploiter. De ce point, il trouve que l'Afrique a un potentiel qu'on ne trouve pas ailleurs. Mais, a-t-il relevé, cette abondance contraste avec la place occupée par le continent dans les circuits économiques mondiaux. Malgré l’importance de ses ressources, l’Afrique reste, selon l’universitaire, maintenue à la périphérie des lieux de décision et des chaînes de valeur. « C'est un paradoxe que la résilience transformatrice nous invite peut-être à essayer de dépasser », a-t-il affirmé, appelant les États africains à mieux valoriser leurs ressources, à préserver leurs richesses naturelles et à renforcer leur capacité à peser sur les choix économiques qui les concernent. Aliou DIOUF

items.title: Plateau – Troops arrest arms fabricator, three suspected gunrunners
items.description: By Golok Nanmwa, Jos Troops of Operation Enduring Peace (OPEP) have arrested an alleged illegal arms fabricator and three suspected gunrunners during coordinated covert operations in Mangu and Barkin Ladi Local Government Areas of Plateau State. Our correspondent gathered that the arrests followed intelligence received by the Headquarters of OPEP on October 4 on the activities of suspected illegal arms fabricators and gunrunners operating in the two local government areas. Consequently, the troops conducted coordinated covert operations between October 7 and 11, targeting the suspected criminal networks and their operational locations. A military source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the operations led to the arrest of an alleged arms fabricator, identified as Ayuba Sunday Abot, who was reportedly operating in Heipang, Barkin Ladi LGA. The source said three other suspects, identified as Tangkat Danjuma, Kopdi Appollos and Nyam Nzang, were also arrested over their alleged involvement in illegal arms trafficking in Mangu and Barkin Ladi LGAs. According to the source, the troops recovered one fabricated revolver rifle, one fabricated pistol, one fabricated AK-47 barrel and one AK-47 magazine during the operations. The source added that 42 rounds of 7.62 mm x 54 mm rimmed ball ammunition were also recovered, alongside materials described in the operational report as metaphysical items. He said preliminary interrogation of the suspects indicated that they allegedly purchased the ammunition at N3,000 per round from a security agent. The spokesman of Operation Enduring Peace, Captain Chinonso Polycarp Oteh, also confirmed the arrests to Vanguard. Oteh said the suspects and all the recovered items had been taken to the Headquarters of Operation Enduring Peace for further investigation. items.title: Burkina Faso : La CNLF met la main sur plus de 55,2 millions de F CFA de marchandises frauduleuses
items.description: La Coordination nationale de lutte contre la fraude (CNLF) a présenté, ce lundi 12 octobre 2026, plusieurs marchandises saisies au cours d’opérations menées les 30 septembre et 1er octobre. Du cyanure, des cigarettes de contrebande, du gasoil subventionné détourné et de l’huile lubrifiante contrefaite figurent parmi les produits concernés. La valeur totale des marchandises saisies et des produits impliqués dans ces affaires est estimée à 55 233 000 F CFA. La lutte contre la fraude se poursuit au Burkina Faso. En l’espace de 48 heures, les équipes de la Coordination nationale de lutte contre la fraude (CNLF) ont démantelé plusieurs circuits de commercialisation illicite et de détournement de produits réglementés. Les opérations ont permis de mettre au jour trois affaires distinctes sur l’axe Ouagadougou-Koupéla, à Loumbila et dans le quartier Patte d’Oie, à Ouagadougou. Présentant les résultats de ces interventions, le coordonnateur national de lutte contre la fraude, le Dr Mohamadi Compaoré, a salué la vigilance des équipes et la contribution des populations. « En l’espace de 48 heures seulement (les 30 septembre et 1er octobre 2026), nos équipes ont asséné un coup dur aux réseaux de fraude, de contrebande et de trafic illicite qui sapent l’économie nationale et menacent notre sécurité », a-t-il déclaré. Cyanure et cigarettes de contrebande sur l’axe Ouaga-Koupéla La première saisie concerne un camion bâché, officiellement chargé de transporter du clinker. Le 1er octobre 2026, une alerte a conduit les agents de la CNLF à procéder à une fouille du véhicule sur l’axe Ouagadougou-Koupéla. L’inspection a permis de découvrir 50 sacs de cyanure de 50 kg chacun, soit 2,5 tonnes de cette substance chimique hautement toxique et réglementée. La valeur de ce produit est estimée à 7,5 millions FCFA. Les agents ont également découvert 15 colis de cigarettes de contrebande, évalués à 3,45 millions FCFA. La valeur totale de cette saisie s’élève à 10,95 millions FCFA. La présence de cyanure dans une cargaison dissimulée soulève notamment des préoccupations liées à la manipulation et à la circulation de substances dangereuses. 59 000 litres de gasoil subventionné détournés à Loumbila Le 30 septembre 2026, sur la base d’un renseignement, les agents de la CNLF ont intercepté un camion-citerne qui venait de décharger 10 000 litres de gasoil dans les cuves d'une unité industrielle. Or, selon le coordonnateur national, le bon de commande présenté était destiné à l’approvisionnement ordinaire des stations-service. Le Dr Mohamadi Compaoré a rappelé que, conformément à un arrêté portant composition des structures de prix des hydrocarbures, le gasoil subventionné par l’État ne peut être utilisé par les mines, les carrières et les entreprises industrielles. Les investigations complémentaires ont permis d’établir, selon la CNLF, que 59 000 litres de gasoil subventionné avaient été cumulés et fournis illégalement à cette entreprise par une société de droit burkinabè. La valeur de ce volume est estimée à 31 683 000 FCFA. Pour le coordonnateur national, cette pratique constitue un détournement de ressources destinées à soutenir les ménages, au profit d’intérêts industriels privés. 267 cartons d’huile lubrifiante contrefaite saisis à Ouagadougou La troisième opération s’est déroulée le 1er octobre 2026 dans le quartier Patte d’Oie, à Ouagadougou. À la suite d’une alerte citoyenne, les agents de la CNLF ont intercepté un véhicule suspect transportant 267 cartons d’huile lubrifiante contrefaite, importés en contrebande. La valeur de la marchandise est estimée à 12,6 millions FCFA. Au-delà du préjudice économique, la commercialisation de produits lubrifiants contrefaits peut compromettre le bon fonctionnement et la durabilité des engins et véhicules. « Nous tenons à saluer le civisme des populations dont les renseignements permettent ces coups de filet », Dr Mohamadi Compaoré Au terme de ces trois opérations, la valeur totale des marchandises saisies et des produits impliqués dans les affaires présentées est estimée à 55,233 millions FCFA. Ce montant comprend les 10,95 millions FCFA de produits prohibés et de cigarettes de contrebande, les 31,683 millions FCFA de gasoil subventionné détourné et les 12,6 millions FCFA d’huile lubrifiante contrefaite. La CNLF entend poursuivre ses actions contre les pratiques frauduleuses qui portent atteinte à l’économie nationale, à la sécurité et à la santé publique. « Ces résultats démontrent que la CNLF ne faiblira pas face à ceux qui tentent d’enrichir leurs affaires au mépris de la loi, de la santé publique et de l’effort national », a affirmé le Dr Mohamadi Compaoré. Le coordonnateur national a également salué la contribution des citoyens dans le signalement des activités suspectes. « Nous tenons à saluer le civisme des populations dont les renseignements permettent ces coups de filet », a-t-il ajouté. À travers cet appel, la CNLF invite les populations à maintenir leur vigilance et à contribuer, par leurs renseignements, à la lutte contre la fraude et les circuits de commercialisation illicite. Faso7 L’article Burkina Faso : La CNLF met la main sur plus de 55,2 millions de F CFA de marchandises frauduleuses est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Les Lionnes visent le troisième tour face à la Tunisie, ce soir
items.description: Victorieuses (1-0) à l’aller à Radès, les Lionnes du Sénégal reçoivent la Tunisie ce mardi 13 octobre 2026 à 17 heures, au stade Léopold Sédar Senghor. Les joueuses d’Abatalib Fall devront préserver leur avantage pour décrocher leur qualification au troisième tour des éliminatoires des JO de Los Angeles 2028. C’est aujourd’hui, mardi, que les Lionnes du Sénégal retrouvent les Aiglonnes de Carthage de la Tunisie pour le match retour du deuxième tour des éliminatoires africaines des Jeux olympiques de Los Angeles 2028. Victorieuses à l’aller (1-0) à Radès, les Sénégalaises tenteront de confirmer leur avantage et de décrocher leur qualification pour le troisième tour, à domicile. Le coup d’envoi de la rencontre est prévu à 17 heures au stade Léopold Sédar Senghor, où les joueuses sénégalaises pourront compter sur le soutien de leur public pour franchir cette nouvelle étape vers les Jeux olympiques. Un peu moins d’une semaine après leur succès en terre tunisienne, les joueuses dirigées par Abatalib Fall abordent cette seconde manche avec une courte avance. Un avantage qu’elles devront défendre avec sérieux face à une sélection nord-africaine déterminée à renverser la situation. Si les Sénégalaises ont pris une option sur la qualification grâce à leur victoire à l’extérieur, elles devront néanmoins rester concentrées jusqu’au coup de sifflet final pour éviter toute mauvaise surprise. À l’aller, Ndèye Awa Casset avait inscrit l’unique but de la rencontre à la 63e minute, offrant aux Lionnes une précieuse victoire et un avantage considérable à l’extérieur. Cette réalisation permet aux Sénégalaises d’aborder le match retour dans une position favorable, même si rien n’est encore acquis. Les Tunisiennes, contraintes de réagir après leur défaite à domicile, devraient tout mettre en œuvre pour refaire leur retard et relancer leurs chances de qualification. L’enjeu sera de préserver leur avantage tout en cherchant à mettre en difficulté leurs adversaires. Devant leur public, les Lionnes auront ainsi l’occasion de confirmer le résultat obtenu à Radès et de poursuivre leur parcours dans ces éliminatoires africaines. Fama NDIAYE

items.title: Des familles toujours dans l’attente d’une issue
items.description: Le Collectif des détenteurs de titres dénonce l’enlisement du dossier foncier lotissement « Hangar Pèlerin » de l’aéroport Dakar-Yoff et annonce une série d’actions de sensibilisation et de mobilisation. Dans un communiqué publié le 11 octobre,il réclame des mesures concrètes de l’État ainsi qu’un calendrier précis pour sortir de l’impasse. Le dossier du lotissement « Hangar Pèlerin » de l’aéroport de Dakar-Yoff reste sans issue définitive au grand désarroi des familles qui y ont investi leurs économies dans l’espoir d’accéder à la propriété. Dans un communiqué publié le 11 octobre, le Collectif des détenteurs de titres interpelle les autorités et annonce une série d’actions destinées à sensibiliser l’opinion publique sur les conséquences humaines, sociales et financières de ce blocage. Depuis plusieurs années, les personnes concernées vivent dans l’incertitude, entre démarches administratives et engagements qui tardent à se concrétiser. Malgré les sollicitations adressées aux autorités, aucune décision définitive n’a permis de clarifier leur situation. Pour ces détenteurs de titres, l’attente se prolonge au prix de sacrifices financiers et de projets familiaux suspendus. Le Collectif dit saluer l’attention accordée par le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, à la gouvernance foncière et à la protection des droits des citoyens. Les démarches entreprises auprès de l’administration n’ont pas permis de dénouer le dossier. Le Collectif rappelle avoir adressé des correspondances au ministre des Finances et du Budget les 21 août 2024 et 23 juin 2025, ainsi qu’au chef de l’État et au directeur des Domaines en juin 2025. L’annonce faite lors du Conseil des ministres du 12 mars 2025 avait pourtant laissé entrevoir une issue. La clôture du processus de vérification du site de Hangar Pèlerin était alors annoncée pour la fin du mois de juin 2025. Mais cette échéance est passée sans qu’une solution définitive soit apportée, nourrissant la déception des détenteurs de titres. Outre ces procédures administratives, le Collectif met en avant la détresse des ménages concernés. Ses membres ne sont pas des spéculateurs fonciers, mais des citoyens qui ont engagé leurs économies, parfois contracté des prêts ou consenti d’importants sacrifices pour acquérir une parcelle. L’absence de dénouement pèse lourdement sur leur quotidien. Face à l’impasse, l’organisation prévoit une série d’actions d’information et de mobilisation citoyenne. Pathé NIANG

items.title: Choose Your Overlord
items.description: T he Adriatic has been crossed by Odysseus and Caesar, by Venetian fleets and Napoleon’s navy, by countless men bent on dominating the world. It has seen its share of courage and folly. But one day in June 2025, off the island of Cres, it witnessed something genuinely new: a man worth $240 billion standing waist-deep in bubbles on the deck of a $500 million yacht, wearing a white bucket hat. The man is Jeff Bezos, and the woman photographed in the string bikini next to him—hugging him, rubbing him with bubbles—is his fiancée, Lauren Sánchez. Bezos is shirtless, and it must be said: He is ripped. His hairless torso is so buff, his expression so amused, that he looks more like a louche cartoon character—a Club Med Ninja Turtle—than a 61-year-old corporate executive. In the foreground, an anonymous crew member, his face hidden from view and his thoughts forever unknown, mans a cannon blasting bubbles into the Croatian sky. The foam party was a birthday celebration for Sánchez’s 19-year-old son, a prelude to the Bezos-Sánchez wedding five days later in Venice—with 200 VIP guests, hundreds of protesters, and an estimated cost of $50 million. The wedding consumed the internet for a week and was treated as a self-contained cultural event, a thing worth interrogating or gawking at on its own terms. In fact it was the culmination of one of the weirder decades that any American billionaire has ever had. The whole republic, to be fair, has been pretty nuts, and Bezos has been both caught up in the insanity and an agent of its acceleration. In 2013, Bezos, who founded Amazon and still owns roughly 8 percent of the company, purchased The Washington Post for $250 million . Two years later, Donald Trump accused him of using the paper as a tax shelter, to which Bezos jokingly responded that Trump should be launched into space. Trump then said at a rally, “If I become president, oh, do they have problems.” Trump became president, and the Pentagon steered a massive cloud-computing contract away from Amazon Web Services, while Trump repeatedly pressured the U.S. Postal Service to raise Amazon’s shipping rates. In 2019, Bezos and his wife, MacKenzie, announced their decision to divorce. A month later, Bezos accused the National Enquirer ’s parent company of attempted extortion after he said it threatened to release intimate photos, including what its chief content officer described in an email as a “below the belt selfie—otherwise colloquially known as a ‘d*ck pick.’ ” (The company said it had “acted lawfully” but would conduct its own investigation.) This is how much of the world learned about Lauren Sánchez, which was awkward because her brother Michael, a court later determined, had spoken with the tabloid about his sister’s relationship and sold—for $200,000—information, text messages, and a number of Bezos’s “ ‘racy,’ ‘explicit’ photos.” Bezos suggested, without evidence, that the plot had been instigated by the Trump administration and the Saudi government in retaliation for the Post ’s reporting on the murder of its columnist Jamal Khashoggi by the Saudis. That’s already a lot, even by billionaire standards. Bezos then stepped down as CEO of Amazon in 2021; went to space aboard a rocket built by Blue Origin, the aerospace company he’d quietly founded two decades earlier; and began devoting the majority of his time to the company. Over roughly the same period, he commissioned the world’s largest sailing yacht and worked on building a 10,000-year clock inside a mountain. By the time of his second wedding, Bezos had transformed physically and politically—killing a Post endorsement of Kamala Harris for president, attending Donald Trump’s second inauguration in a seat of honor, reorienting the paper’s Opinion section around “personal liberties and free markets,” cheerleading Amazon’s reported $40 million deal for a documentary and future docuseries about Melania Trump. People change. And if Bezos were just another middle-aged guy using his money to become unrecognizable to his former self—God bless. Enjoy the Met Gala. But we live in a society where trivializing the actions of our wealthiest citizens is both unbeatable fun and a form of recklessness. For most of the past decade, the changes in Bezos that attracted attention were the meme-able ones: his body, his partner, his yacht. This made the transformation that mattered harder to see. We’ve been gawking at Bezos becoming a different kind of billionaire while missing his attempt to become a different kind of historical figure. The man who once rewired how the planet buys and sells everything has been chasing an even grander project—creating the infrastructure for an off-world economy upon which human civilization might someday depend. If this sounds implausible and potentially menacing, you will not be surprised to learn that the person standing between Bezos and his ambition is the implausible and menacing Elon Musk , who has spent the past two decades building a commanding lead in space while pursuing a different vision of where humanity should go once it gets there. Together, in fierce competition, these two billionaires are in the early stages of a race to vertically integrate the galaxy—a process that involves rockets, moon landings, enormous satellite constellations, and space-based data centers running AI models fueled by computing power that no terrestrial supplier can match. Both say they hope to preserve human life from the specter of climate change and expand mankind’s understanding of the universe. Both would also like to dominate a market that, unlike every other market they’ve previously conquered, has no ceiling and few established rules. Whether any of this is wise is a question the rest of us are not really being asked. For most of human history, the power to decide where a civilization went next belonged to governments, monarchs, or despots. It’s a measure of how much has changed that a retail executive from Seattle and a South African–born engineer are well positioned to exercise that power. Nobody voted for either of them. And they may be the only ones who can check the other’s power. Jake Sullivan, Joe Biden’s national security adviser, described this to me as “a very weird situation.” You’ve got two men with unfathomable power and an unshakable faith that they’re destined to shape the world. But neither of them is “actually Lex Luthor,” Sullivan said. “ … Right?” Perhaps not. But any answer requires a deeper understanding of the two men involved. Musk, typically, has overshared. Bezos has been more secretive. To reveal his character and intent, you first have to get past the foam. In the 1990s, when reporters began tracing the origin story of the first king of e-commerce, they made their way to Miami, where Bezos grew up, and to Ursula Werner, his high-school girlfriend. They had listened to ABBA together and he’d made her adoring flyers for her birthday, and she told those reporters something about him that, for years, seemed like just another cute bit of color: “The reason he’s earning so much money,” Werner said, “is to get to outer space.” Chris Carroll / Getty Jeff Bezos in 1999 In his high-school-valedictorian speech, Bezos quoted Star Trek —“Space, the final frontier”—and asked his audience to imagine vast orbital colonies where humanity could relocate Earth’s most polluting industries, an idea cooked up by the Princeton physicist Gerard K. O’Neill in the 1970s. “The earth is finite,” Bezos explained to a local reporter. “And if the world economy and population is to keep expanding, space is the only way to go.” All of this nerd enthusiasm was out in the open until 2000, when Bezos created Blue Origin Enterprises. He based the company a short commute from Amazon’s Seattle headquarters and kept its existence a secret for three years, until Newsweek discovered it. This was not the only strange thing about Blue Origin. For a while, the company’s sole employee was the science-fiction writer Neal Stephenson, best known for Snow Crash , a 1992 novel set in a near-future America where the government has collapsed and corporations run everything. In a blog post, Stephenson wrote that his title at Blue Origin was “Member, Technical Staff,” and that he “performed operations as prosaic as punching down Ethernet cable, operating a plate grinder, and passivating rocket parts.” But that was just part of the job. “The bulk of my efforts,” Stephenson wrote, “were devoted to investigating possible alternatives to conventional rockets.” Bezos wanted to know if almost a century of rocket science had gotten the basic question wrong—whether there was a smarter way to get to space than attaching a tube to massive amounts of fuel and setting it all on fire. Stephenson and the handful of other employees who were eventually hired ran software simulations that would either validate the conventional approach or, Bezos hoped, find its replacement. This is a pretty wild way to spend your money. Three years of experiments proved that Wernher von Braun and Robert Goddard hadn’t missed anything. Only then did Bezos hire the former NASA engineer Rob Meyerson and buy 165,000 acres of Texas scrub brush where rocket prototypes might someday be launched without scrutiny. Eventually Meyerson would be promoted to president—but of what, exactly? In the early years, Blue Origin had no customers or finished product, and little of what ordinarily makes a company a business. Bezos left the CEO job vacant and imposed no conventional timetable. It did have a tortoise mascot and a motto—“ Gradatim ferociter ” (“Step by step, ferociously”)—that reinforced its commitment to getting to space slowly, secretly, and stubbornly. Employees were focused on whiteboarding a tourism rocket, but Bezos told Meyerson not to worry about sales or pitching government agencies; he didn’t want to be held hostage by customers. It was “a science experiment for the first 15 years,” Tom Jones, Blue Origin’s vice president of human resources from 2016 to 2019, told me. Contrast this with the hyper-logical way that Bezos had conceived Amazon . In an early interview, Bezos explained that the internet was growing at 2,300 percent a year; to capitalize on that growth, he needed a product category with more variety than any physical store could stock. There were more than 3 million active book titles worldwide. Therefore: books. If Amazon was the company that Mr. Spock would create, Blue Origin was where Bezos got to lead with his heart and be Captain Kirk. He’d take days off from Amazon for field trips, packing Blue Origin employees onto his private plane and dropping in on companies with cultures or engineering accomplishments that he admired. Gradually, Bezos cleared all of his Wednesday afternoons and many of his Saturdays to work at the Blue Origin office. When Bezos wanted to learn about heat-transfer codes—software that models how heat moves through a rocket engine; the difference between an engine that survives its own combustion and one that doesn’t—Meyerson hired an employee to tutor him. I asked Meyerson if managing Bezos’s enthusiasm ever got in the way of accelerating Blue Origin’s progress. “My job was to do both,” he said. “The time that he put into Blue was a gift to us, because the more he understood, the more he was willing to support what was needed for the long run.” And yet, when it came to money, the accountant overruled the dreamer. Bezos was rich— Forbes ’s 100th-wealthiest American—but not send-my-money-to-the-moon rich. He didn’t want “to spend the kind of money he’s spending today,” Meyerson said. Blue Origin would work through simulations, models, and small prototypes—staying within its means until Bezos was ready to scale up. This would have been fine if Blue Origin were operating in a vacuum. But two years after Bezos founded his dream company, someone else started a company with a dream just as large. And he was not interested in moving slowly. Impatience is part of Elon Musk’s mystique. So is an eagerness to break and remake things: the economics of car buying (Tesla), the operations of the federal government (DOGE), the last remaining norms of social media (X—now a platform for disturbing racial theories). But Musk didn’t set out to revolutionize aerospace and become the world’s most successful rocket builder. Originally he just wanted to be a rocket buyer. Dan Tuffs / Getty Elon Musk in 2008 with an early model of SpaceX’s Dragon capsule, designed to carry a crew or cargo into space atop a rocket In 2001, Musk announced that he would send a robotic greenhouse into space, scoop up some Martian soil, and use it to grow a plant. This scientific publicity stunt may not go down as Musk’s best idea, but his attempt to buy refurbished intercontinental ballistic missiles for the Martian-soil gambit led him to Moscow, where, according to Ashlee Vance’s biography, Elon Musk , a Russian engineer spat on him (literally) and his PayPal millions. Flying back from a second unsuccessful trip, Musk opened a spreadsheet and realized that he could build a rocket for less than the $8 million the Russians wanted to charge him to buy one—and for less than anyone had ever built a rocket before. He founded SpaceX a month later. It’s easy in hindsight, and with this year’s $1.8 trillion SpaceX IPO , to say that Musk had a better plan than Bezos to get to space. What’s inarguable is that Musk had a faster plan. He staffed up by cold-calling college aerospace students and handing them ludicrous deadlines—the first launch was scheduled for 15 months after the company was created. Speed gave SpaceX swagger, and that swagger gave its young employees faith. But the company’s most important virtue was thrift. Not as a means of preserving Musk’s wealth, but because lowering costs was the entire point of the business. For decades, getting a person or a satellite into orbit was so expensive that only governments and the largest defense contractors could afford it. Musk believed that this had little to do with physics; unlike Bezos, he spent no time wondering whether there might be a fundamentally different way to get to space. Instead, he looked at launch costs the way a deregulator might have looked at long-distance telephone rates in the 1970s: not as a law of nature, but as the product of the people who had gotten there first and decided what to charge. If SpaceX could create a reusable rocket capable of driving launch costs down far enough, it wouldn’t just swallow all the existing demand—it would transform space from a cartel into a free market. Satellite builders, scientists, start-ups, and, eventually, anyone with a payload and a business case could participate. Access to space would become as abundant as telephony. And then all sorts of innovation might happen. Bezos had a similar vision, and both men believed that reusable rockets were the key to making space affordable. But while Blue Origin was moving step by step, SpaceX skipped every step it could. Employees were celebrated for outrageous hacks, such as figuring out that off-the-shelf car-wash valves worked just fine for rockets if you swapped their seals. All of that ingenuity led to Musk’s promise that SpaceX’s first rocket, Falcon 1, would carry a 1,400-pound payload into orbit for $6.9 million—75 percent less than any competitor. He nearly went bankrupt doing it. The first three Falcon launches failed. By 2008, SpaceX and Tesla were burning cash. Musk was barely solvent enough to make one more launch attempt. On September 28, Falcon 1 reached orbit, making SpaceX the first privately funded company to launch a liquid-fueled rocket into space. The timing was exquisite. Three months later, as the global financial system teetered and Musk was days away from missing payroll, NASA awarded SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract to resupply the International Space Station. The company had gone from near death to indispensable in a single quarter. A former senior NASA official who visited both companies in their early years described Blue Origin to me as an academic lab and SpaceX as a pirate ship. “SpaceX was scrappy,” the official said. “I went to the Blue factories in Kent, Washington, and they were these beautiful, massive buildings with the world’s best 3‑D printers. And I was like, Where are the people? Then you go to SpaceX in Hawthorne, and there’s these young people running around; everybody’s greasy.” The differences were hardly lost on the people watching from Blue Origin. SpaceX had taken Amazon’s “get big fast” playbook and applied it to rockets⁠—staffing up, sprinting to deadlines, and treating its failures as content rather than embarrassment. The launch explosions and misfires it shared on social media didn’t make SpaceX look reckless; they made it look humble. At Blue Origin, the contrast was unmistakable: SpaceX seemed to be having more fun. SpaceX soon proved that it could reuse rocket boosters—the bottom part where the flames shoot out. Its first reusable rocket, Falcon 9, launched and landed in 2015. By May 2016, SpaceX was on its way to becoming the UPS of low Earth orbit. Satellite customers could buy launches at published prices, and Falcon 9 was beginning to fly on something approaching a regular schedule. NASA was already relying on SpaceX to shuttle cargo to the International Space Station; the Air Force had certified Falcon 9 for national-security missions and had just awarded the company its first military-launch contract. In West Texas, Blue Origin was completing the first takeoffs and landings of its New Shepard tourism rocket. Those missions were uncrewed and suborbital—which is to say, the rocket went to space the way a ball tossed upward in a backyard goes above the roofline: fleetingly. On Twitter, Musk pointed out how far ahead SpaceX was, beginning a series of exchanges in which two of the world’s richest men engaged in public rocket-measuring contests. Musk won most of these, which makes sense, because Musk was winning. People who have worked closely with Bezos bring up two defining characteristics. The first is a comfort, bordering on delight, at being misunderstood. “I think he enjoys it,” a former Amazon senior executive told me. “You have no idea how stubborn he can be in defense of an idea only he believes. And of course a lot of times he’s right.” The second is that Bezos does not like multitasking. He’s told audiences that as a little kid in Montessori school, he was so resistant to leaving things undone that he had to be picked up in his chair and moved to the next activity. Bezos prefers to direct his focus, as intensely as possible, on one problem at a time. As long as he remained the CEO of Amazon, that problem was Amazon. For the first 15 years of Blue Origin’s existence, the company had to accommodate that reality. Whether it was Musk’s taunts or the unignorable fact that SpaceX was racing ahead, Bezos finally changed course in 2016. During one of his regular Saturday meetings at Blue Origin, he asked a question that nobody in the room wanted to answer honestly: Why hadn’t Blue Origin directly bid on an Air Force contract for rocket-engine development that had just gone to SpaceX? The answer: Because you’ve always told us not to . Bezos delivered a new mandate to Meyerson: “From now on, we go after everything that SpaceX bids on.” When people in aerospace talk about SpaceX’s advantages, they nod to Musk’s maniacal expectations, his engineering instincts, and the particular quality of his attention. But Musk’s attention has at times been distributed across Tesla, X, the neurotechnology company Neuralink, the tunnel start-up the Boring Company, the federal government, and 14 children by four women. Musk’s life is a browser with too many tabs. X is the tab that’s always open . It’s where he challenged Mark Zuckerberg to a cage match, offered to give Taylor Swift a child and guard her cats “with my life,” and feuded with (partial list) Kanye West, the British government, the Australian government, the Brazilian supreme court, and a cave diver in Thailand he called a “pedo guy”—leading to a defamation lawsuit that Musk won after his legal team argued that the phrase was a generic insult. It’s also where he regularly posts memes and has promoted anti-Semitic content that makes him, justifiably, a pariah among people who believe society is plenty coarse enough without him. (SpaceX did not respond to interview requests for this story.) The point is, Musk is no more focused than Bezos. The difference is that he’s never needed to be. This is because, in 2002, he had a three-minute conversation with Gwynne Shotwell. Shotwell is 62, and remarkable in several ways—a woman in a male-dominated field, a proud former high-school cheerleader with degrees in mechanical engineering and applied mathematics. But her unique gift is the ability to read her boss’s mind while ignoring his id. “I like his in-person self better than his Twitter self,” Shotwell said in a 2022 talk at Stanford . Shotwell is self-aware and funny. Not aerospace funny—actually funny. She grew up in the “boonies” north of Chicago and was a sophomore in high school when her mother dropped her off at a Society of Women Engineers event. She decided to become a mechanical engineer that day in part because one of the presenters “had the best suit on, and she had great shoes, and her bag matched her shoes,” Shotwell told a podcast interviewer with delight. Shotwell was in the middle of a career in traditional aerospace when she went to lunch with a former co-worker who had been poached by SpaceX. She was introduced to Musk on a tour of the office, and received a job offer to be vice president of business development that afternoon. For weeks she hesitated before pulling over on the Los Angeles freeway, calling Musk, and telling him that she was an “effing idiot” for not accepting sooner. He laughed and welcomed her to the team. Since then, Shotwell and Musk have built one of the most drama-free partnerships in 21st-century business. He oversees engineering and technology while she takes care of everything else—sales, operations, manufacturing, workforce vibes. While Musk was supervising the 2008 do-or-die Falcon-rocket launch, Shotwell was at an industry conference in Glasgow, watching the livestream at 2 a.m. in her hotel room while writing the company’s bid to resupply the International Space Station. When the rocket reached orbit, she ran down the hallway to rouse her colleagues and broke into the hotel bar to drink warm champagne. In 2015, having proved that SpaceX could reliably deliver payloads to space, Musk announced plans for a constellation of thousands of satellites, now known as Starlink. The pitch had a noble dimension—SpaceX would bring high-speed internet to parts of the world that fiber-optic cables had left behind. But this disguised its real purpose. SpaceX’s first act—flying rockets for hire—was not profitable enough. Getting in on boring old telecommunications would give the company a way to monetize its own launch capability. Starlink was created to be the thing that would pay for everything else. The following year, Musk revealed the full scope of his plan: SpaceX would build a fully reusable two-stage rocket and spacecraft standing just over 400 feet tall and powered by 42 engines, with a capsule—the top part—capable of carrying 100 people to Mars (or 60 Starlink satellites into orbit). “The objective is to become a spacefaring civilization and a multiplanet species,” Musk said at the time. “The main reason I’m personally accumulating assets is to fund this.” Previous spacecraft carried only what they needed for a mission. This would be like launching a Costco. Scale is the great paradox of rocket science. A rocket twice as large as its predecessor isn’t just twice as hard to build; as the rocket grows, so do the forces trying to tear it apart. At the size Musk envisioned, the fully fueled vehicle would weigh more than 10 million pounds, more than one and a half times the weight of the Saturn V, which carried astronauts to the moon. Lifting it would require engines more powerful than anything SpaceX had built before, with roughly three times the pressure of the engines powering its Falcon rockets—conditions so extreme that SpaceX would need to invent new manufacturing techniques simply to build the combustion chamber. And Musk intended to reuse everything: Both the giant booster and the spacecraft above it would return to Earth and fly again. The design would change repeatedly—first landing legs, then enormous mechanical arms—but the economic premise remained the same. If full and rapid reuse worked, Musk believed that the cost of reaching orbit could eventually fall below $100 a kilogram, which would make the things that had always died on a spreadsheet—lunar bases, enormous satellite constellations, perhaps even human flights to Mars—possible. The architecture was elegant in its circularity. Starship, as the giant rocket and spaceship would come to be known, would make Starlink, the satellite array, far cheaper to deploy. Starlink would then generate revenue to pay for a fleet of Starships. And Starships, eventually, would get humans to Mars. Engineering, commerce, and Musk’s interplanetary ambition, all stacked inside the same rocket. People at Blue Origin first noticed the woman around 2018. She was seen at the Cedarbrook Lodge near the Seattle airport, a few minutes before Bezos arrived for drinks with executives. In West Texas, she began showing up as a contractor on the helicopter video team that documented New Shepard launches. Lauren Sánchez Bezos is impossible not to notice because her lifelong goal, exuberantly pursued, is to be noticed. Sánchez Bezos grew up in New Mexico, learned she was dyslexic in community college, hustled her way into the University of Southern California, and for several years proceeded through the carnival of gigs (local news, Extra , So You Think You Can Dance ) available to attractive and relentless people who want to be on television. She had a child with the former NFL tight end Tony Gonzalez before marrying Patrick Whitesell, the Hollywood agent and power broker, with whom she had two more children. In 2016, she got her helicopter pilot’s license and started an aerial-production company. The first public encounter between Bezos and Lauren Sánchez was at a December 2016 Amazon Studios party for the grim kids-die-in-a-fire movie Manchester by the Sea . It must have been like meeting Jayne Mansfield at a shiva. Both were married at the time, and what happened next seems clear enough, even without the benefit of any photos from the National Enquirer . “Wonderful madness” is how Barry Diller, the media mogul and Bezos’s close friend, describes the relationship. Understanding the force and fury of the response to the couple requires some unpacking, and it starts with the woman Bezos left. MacKenzie Scott studied creative writing at Princeton under Toni Morrison, did Amazon’s early bookkeeping out of Bezos’s garage, and has spent the years since their 2019 divorce giving away her share of the proceeds—more than $26 billion to more than 2,000 organizations—while largely erasing any evidence of her generosity. In August, she released a complicated third novel on Substack. “I have great respect for and fondness for MacKenzie,” Diller told me. “You can see how she’s conducting her charitable work, which is remarkable—but it’s all quiet and private. And that’s MacKenzie.” J.
