She’s written three children’s books— The Fly Who Flew to Space , The Fly Who Flew Under the Sea , and The Fly Who Flew to the North Pole —and if a brick wall were the only thing standing between her and the best-seller list, you wouldn’t want to be the wall. “People assume she’s going to be Cruella, and she’s not,” a woman who’s been friends with Sánchez Bezos for a decade told me. “She’s smart and kind, and she has real accomplishments. But it’s confusing because snobby people look at her big, vulgar boobs, and she’s like, Yeah! Look at ’em! She likes being sexy. She just wants everyone to have a good time, and she doesn’t mind being the good time.” Bezos and Sánchez Bezos make each other happy. This is not nothing, but the wonderful madness has had its costs. There was an alleged blackmail attempt to manage, a 25-year marriage to unwind, and a company that still depended on Bezos’s attention. The scandal “had a huge impact at Blue Origin,” Alexandra Abrams, the former head of employee communications, told me. (Abrams, who was fired in 2019, later went public with complaints about flight safety and criticized leadership, Bezos included, for what she described as a “toxic” culture; in response, the company said it had no tolerance for discrimination or harassment and stood by its safety record.) Abrams said that the news of Bezos’s relationship with Sánchez “started to break the goodwill of a lot of the senior employees at the company. They were shocked that Jeff would comport himself in that way.” Only Bezos can say how much of his transformation has been driven or enabled by his new wife, and how much was always there, waiting for permission. And Bezos, who declined multiple requests for an interview, isn’t talking. A few weeks after the Manchester by the Sea party, Trump’s NASA transition team invited Blue Origin to a meeting. With Bezos’s decree to start competing, Bretton Alexander, the director of business development and strategy, scrambled to prepare. Mike Pence was passionate about space. Trump understood the MAGA value of rockets and astronauts. So, the transition team asked: What big idea could Blue Origin offer that would be ready by the electorally convenient date of 2020? “I didn’t see the question coming,” Alexander told me. But he blurted out, “We’ve landed New Shepard in the desert five times in the last year. We can land something on the moon, because we have the engines and we have the technology.” The last person to walk on the moon was the Apollo 17 commander, Gene Cernan , who let a crewmate climb the ladder before him so that he could utter the following: “We leave as we came and, God willing, as we shall return, with peace and hope for all mankind.” That was in 1972. There’s no single explanation for why America hasn’t returned, but there are several timely reasons to go back. The moon is the most convenient place in the cosmos: three days away, without the communication lags that make deep-space operations so complicated. It has water-ice deposits , which theoretically could sustain human life and be split into hydrogen and oxygen, also known as rocket fuel. And because the moon’s gravity is one-sixth of Earth’s, less fuel is required to launch from its surface and explore the rest of the solar system. For 4.5 billion years, celestial objects have used the moon as target practice, enriching the lunar soil with most every rare mineral the solar system has produced. Half its face is shielded from Earth’s electromagnetic noise, which makes it valuable for radio telescopes and, as national-security officials will warn in varying degrees of specificity, potentially useful to America’s adversaries. The Chinese have committed to landing astronauts on the moon by 2030. For all of these reasons, Alexander’s pitch appealed to the transition team. That it nudged federal space policy toward the moon—elevating Bezos’s high-school dreams while usurping Musk, who hoped the Trump administration would back a Mars mission—was, for Blue Origin, the chef’s kiss. Alexander called Rob Meyerson right away. “I said, ‘Oh shit, I just created a program.’ ” Greg Autry, who now leads international space policy at the State Department, was on the transition team. “We knew they didn’t really have this thing in their garage,” Autry told me. The company had announced New Glenn, its first orbital rocket, earlier that year, but the new rocket had not even carried a commercial payload, let alone human beings. But Blue Origin had “what appeared to be a simple and relatively quick way to get there, with a reusable system.” NASA, perhaps, was also beginning to realize that having a single dominant space-launch provider might in itself be a risk. Animosity continued between Trump and Bezos, who remained publicly critical of the president’s immigration policies. The Pentagon awarded a cloud-computing contract worth up to $10 billion to Microsoft when Amazon Web Services was the undisputed market leader. Amazon sued—and asked for Trump to be deposed, arguing that the president’s dislike of Bezos had corrupted the bidding process. (The Pentagon’s Office of Inspector General found no direct evidence of White House interference but noted that it could not complete its assessment, because senior officials had asserted “presidential communications privilege.” The suit was thrown out in 2021 when a new contract was awarded to both Amazon and Microsoft.) But meaningful friction appears to have stopped at Blue Origin’s door. A few months after Alexander’s meeting, Bezos flew to Washington to personally present his company’s proposal to the transition team. “That didn’t necessarily happen with the other companies,” Autry said. “You didn’t see their CEO or funder take the time to do that.” So began a drip of white papers and study contracts that, over several years, led to $592 million in government funding. Other than a 2019 meeting where Pence’s chief of staff told a Blue Origin executive that the company had a “ Washington Post problem”—a detail later reported in The Washington Post —no one I spoke with could recall an instance when the Trump administration’s hostility toward Bezos translated into prejudice against Blue Origin. There was plenty of turbulence at Blue Origin during this period, but it was self-inflicted, and well overdue. At a Saturday leadership-team meeting in 2017, Bezos was presented with a memo outlining Blue Origin’s annual budget request. Senior leadership wanted more than $1 billion, double the current budget. All of which would come out of Bezos’s pocket. When Bezos finished reading the memo, “he walks out, doesn’t say a word,” Tom Jones, Blue Origin’s former vice president of human resources, told me. “About 15 minutes later, he walks in and he says, ‘Why did I not know that you were going to be making a request this large until today?’ ” Jones described Bezos as calm, even affectionate; Bezos said that he loved the people in the room but that the request was “craziness,” and wildly disproportionate to their achievements. The company had convinced Washington to take its lunar ambitions seriously, but it had yet to put anything into orbit. “It’s probably one of the things that might have led to him thinking, like, Okay, I’ve got to make a change here .” Bezos responded by bringing in Bob Smith, a veteran of the aerospace company Honeywell, as Blue Origin’s first CEO in September 2017. Smith told me he arrived at a company with no steady revenue stream and no supply chain: “Engineers would design a part, put the order out, and then it’d show up by mail back on their desk.” It was essentially “a prototype shop.” Blue Origin might not have had a supply chain, but it did have a cosmology. Bezos “is God at Blue Origin,” Alexandra Abrams said. “Jeff’s big message was that it’s too late for climate-change efforts on Earth, and we need to be able to leave. We need to sustainably go into space and build resources, have a base on the moon, which would act as a gas station to the rest of the solar system. At the company, everyone felt like we were saving humanity.” But God remained an intermittent presence. Bezos had tried to extract himself from Amazon for years—installing deputies, restructuring leadership. COVID wrecked that project; Amazon’s logistics network buckled in the spring of 2020, and Bezos had no choice but to dive back in. Meanwhile, Blue Origin was in the middle of a significant expansion. Bezos had authorized Smith to make thousands of new hires and build new factories, a transformation that required exactly the kind of consistent attention he couldn’t provide. Bezos had made himself indispensable by being the only person who knew exactly what he wanted. He had never found his Gwynne Shotwell—or perhaps he’d never believed the job could be done by someone who wasn’t him. In his absence, Blue Origin was growing fast and bidding on everything, but it was still chronically late. New Glenn, Blue Origin’s version of the Falcon, still wasn’t flying by the time SpaceX began developing Starship. SpaceX announced its Starlink constellation in 2015, put prototypes into orbit in 2018, and began deploying at scale in 2019—at which time Amazon had not yet launched a single prototype for Project Kuiper, its we-can-do-satellites-too Starlink competitor. Bezos wasn’t chasing Musk so much as arriving at places Musk had already left. The pattern held as SpaceX started flying astronauts to the International Space Station. Blue Origin’s answer, when it finally came, was personal. On July 5, 2021, Bezos vacated the CEO seat at Amazon. Two weeks later, he flew to space on New Shepard, the tourism rocket his company had spent years building, alongside his brother, Mark; the aviation pioneer Wally Funk ; and an 18-year-old whose father, a Dutch financier, had bought him a ticket. Bezos stepped out of the capsule in the West Texas heat wearing a cowboy hat and declared it the best day ever. Joe Raedle / Getty Blue Origin’s New Shepard rocket lifting off in 2021, with Bezos aboard The Bezos who returned to Blue Origin was different. He seemed determined to run the company the way he had once run Amazon—present, demanding, involved in every significant decision. Smith’s 2023 resignation took no one by surprise. He had grown Blue Origin from roughly 850 employees to more than 10,000, accumulated billions of dollars in customer orders, and built enormous manufacturing facilities in Huntsville, Alabama, and Cape Canaveral, Florida. But New Glenn continued not to launch. And when NASA, under the Biden administration, finally awarded the contract for its Human Landing System—the moon lander that Bretton Alexander had improvised into existence—it did not go to Blue Origin. SpaceX, proposing a lunar lander based on its Starship architecture, undercut Blue Origin’s $6 billion bid by more than half. What followed was also personal—and a little embarrassing. Blue Origin filed a protest, prompting Musk to tweet, “Can’t get it up (to orbit) lol,” and to offer Bezos some unsolicited management advice. “I think he needs to run BO full-time for it to be successful,” Musk told The Washington Post . “Frankly, I hope he does.” Bezos offered to cover $2 billion of the lunar-lander costs, then $3 billion. When NASA ignored Bezos, Blue Origin sued . Musk, again: “You cannot sue your way to the moon.” The courts agreed. The saga ended when NASA, nudged by Senators Patty Murray and Maria Cantwell of Washington, awarded Blue Origin a $3.4 billion contract to build a competing lander. Bezos decided that the next person to lead Blue Origin didn’t need to understand rockets or politics; they needed to understand him. Dave Limp had run Amazon’s consumer-devices business—Kindle, Echo, Alexa—for nearly 14 years. Limp had also overseen Project Kuiper, where he pushed to spread the risk among multiple launch providers rather than depend on Blue Origin alone. He even said Amazon would be “crazy” not to consider SpaceX, given its track record. In his final interview before accepting the job, Limp asked a single question: Was Blue Origin a hobby or a business? Because if it was a hobby, he wasn’t interested. Bezos told him, “It’s obviously a business. It has to be a business or it’s not going to work.” During the decade when Bezos was reorganizing his life around space, he walked away from a promise he’d made on the day he bought the Post : “The paper’s duty will remain to its readers and not to the private interests of its owners.” The killing of the Harris endorsement, the subscriber cancellations, and the cascade of staff reductions—all of this has been well chronicled, because there’s no beat that journalists swarm quite like a competitor’s newsroom. But the core questions about Bezos and the Post remain: Why does he appear to have inverted his own promise? Was this an act of betrayal or of neglect? And, in the end, is there a difference? When Bezos first showed up in Washington, the paper’s circulation was plummeting. One former Post executive described Bezos’s 2013 arrival to me as a kind of rapture. He was a forceful presence, respectful of the wall between the editorial and business sides, but relentless about improving the customer experience. Those first two years were “absolutely fucking magical,” the former executive told me. The Post went on a sustained run of profitability, and subscriptions surged throughout the first Trump administration. But traffic and urgency declined in the Biden years, while COVID and Bezos’s other interests made him a phantom in Washington. He surfaced to participate in hiring Sally Buzbee to succeed Marty Baron as executive editor in 2021. In 2023, the Post lost $77 million. Bezos surfaced again, to replace the paper’s longtime publisher with Will Lewis, a British-tabloid veteran. There were other candidates—a person close to the hiring process told me that one of them found their conversation with Bezos baffling. The Post ’s owner couldn’t answer basic questions about the newspaper. Bezos seemed inattentive, and said that his priorities would not change: He was focused on Blue Origin and Lauren. Bezos appeared to think that his lack of involvement would be attractive; the next publisher would have free rein. I was a columnist at the Post for a year, and had a few conversations with Lewis early in his tenure. He’d been a journalist before entering the wolf pack of Rupert Murdoch’s executive program, and among his talents was an unusual ability to throw back pints with reporters while keeping the secrets of powerful men. I found him to be a delightful, charismatic scoundrel. Many colleagues were charmed by Lewis. But within a few months, his fury over the newsroom’s coverage of accusations that he’d helped conceal or destroy evidence while managing a scandal at Murdoch’s News International⁠—accusations he has denied—had soured the dynamic. Equally concerning was that Lewis barely demonstrated any interest in his job. The Post lost $100 million in his first year—and an astonishing 60 million monthly visitors from November 2020 to November 2024. But Bezos wasn’t paying much attention to Lewis or the newsroom; he regularly canceled meetings with top editors. Bezos seemed more interested in the Opinion section. He never forbade the editorial board from writing what it wanted, and seldom voiced strong feelings about politicians or parties. But his interests and ideology were evolving, and as the owner, he hoped the editorial board would move in step. Bezos seemed to enjoy speaking with the section’s editor, David Shipley, about creating a forum for pragmatic ideas and policy solutions. Wonky centrist stuff. That hands-off approach changed with the spiking of the Harris endorsement 11 days before the 2024 election—abruptly ending a half-century-long tradition and provoking 250,000 subscription cancellations. Those sympathetic to Bezos say that the last-minute timing wasn’t his fault. Lewis had told the editorial board that he would handle getting Bezos’s approval. But as the election drew closer, it clearly had not been handled—or was not handle-able. “The timing of their refusing to endorse was too close to the election,” Barry Diller told me. “If the Post had been his only job, he would have done that much earlier.” Lewis, who stepped aside in February 2026, did not respond to requests for comment. He certainly deserves blame for some of the destruction. But the most consequential decisions were not his. It was not Lewis who withheld the endorsement. It was not Lewis who complained to Trump about the “terrible” businesspeople at the Post shortly after Trump’s reelection, according to Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s Regime Change . It was not Lewis who dined with the president on the very day he announced that the Opinion section would focus exclusively on “personal liberties and free markets” (a decision that prompted Shipley’s resignation). Bezos has framed the changes at the Post as a matter of necessity and opportunity, writing in an op-ed that he wanted to reposition the paper for Middle America. Journalism isn’t a charity, and Bezos’s own politics have clearly shifted. He is, after all, the owner. Just as Blue Origin was getting its act together, a second Trump presidency dawned, with Bezos’s chief antagonist, Elon Musk, in a position of extraordinary influence. Musk had spent $288 million to help elect Trump and other Republicans. He was a senior adviser to the president. Amazon had fought the first Trump administration for more than a year over a cloud-computing contract. The administration had been lobbied hard by Oracle, Amazon’s cloud competitor, whose co-founder had reportedly given about $45 million to a nonprofit supporting Trump’s reelection. Oracle had also produced a docket of baseless conspiracies about Amazon that found its way to the president’s desk. Marty Baron was the executive editor of the Post from 2013 to 2021, a gilded era that produced 11 Pulitzer Prizes and vital reporting on Edward Snowden, the Trump Access Hollywood tape, and the Robert Mueller investigation. “Everything I saw in my years there was that he truly believed what he was saying about democracy and the press,” Baron told me. “But I don’t think he thinks these other businesses could survive unless he finds a way to successfully navigate through the Trump era. And if the Post is the thing that has to pay the price, then, well, that’ll have to be the thing that pays the price.” Donald Trump is not a simple transactional figure. He gets what he wants, but he also warps reality in the process. Countless executives have learned that successfully dealing with him requires both capitulation and an insistence that no capitulation has occurred. If Bezos and Trump did come to an arrangement, it would make Bezos a hypocrite twice: once for breaking his promise to Post readers, and once for pretending he hadn’t. Jeff Bezos also tends to get what he wants—and unlike Trump, he’s willing to wait years for it. He’s comfortable with being misunderstood. Which is another way of saying that there’s more than one way to look at a Faustian bargain: not in terms of what must be sacrificed, but in terms of what might one day be gained. “NG‑3, baby!” whooped a man in a Titusville, Florida, 7-Eleven in April, shortly before flashing me his admittedly glorious NASA-logo calf tattoo. People who live along Florida’s 72-mile Space Coast rarely end up there by accident. Some work in aerospace; the rest seem to wish they did. They buy condos and arrange their schedules for optimal viewing of the rockets rising from the Kennedy Space Center. As subcultures go, they’re somewhere between Deadheads and bird-watchers: obsessive, migratory, and willing to wait a very long time for the thing they came to see. I was in town at the invitation of Blue Origin to witness the third launch of New Glenn—NG‑3. This would be the first time Blue Origin reused a booster from a previous launch, a crucial step. The nonreusable upper part of NG‑3 would be carrying a large telecom satellite for AST SpaceMobile. Dave Limp was in from Washington State to watch the launch and schmooze the satellite guys. Limp is 60, and in his sensible jeans, glasses, and Blue Origin three-quarter zip, he looks like the most reasonable man in every room he enters. When he started the job, he’d wondered if a consumer-electronics guy was the right fit for a rocket company, but he’d come around to Bezos’s diagnosis—that Blue Origin needed more disciplined decision making, more manufacturing expertise, and more Bezos. “Jeff can be annoying at times, but he’s right a lot,” Limp told me. “And he was right on this.” The standard that Limp is being held to has a name: Gwynne Shotwell. Limp is an admirer, and has arranged his duties accordingly. “My job is to have Jeff live in the future,” Limp said. “So if he has to hear about an HR issue or a financial issue or a schedule issue, I have not done my job.” His other job is to get rockets up, fast. The Federal Communications Commission requires satellite operators such as AST to put a certain percentage of their constellations in space by specific dates, or they risk losing authorization for the satellites they failed to deploy. Amazon was supposed to deploy half of its 3,236 satellites by July 2026. The FCC granted a waiver in June after Amazon explained that it was producing satellites faster than any of its launch providers—including Blue Origin—could get them into space. A year earlier, the New Shepard tourism rocket had carried a team of six women, including Lauren Sánchez and Katy Perry, into space. Now Limp put it on indefinite hiatus. All focus, he told me, was on the lunar lander and getting New Glenn rockets produced with assembly-line speed: “The ‘step by step’ component of our motto—let’s fast-walk it, you know?” At 7:25 a.m. the next morning, NG‑3 lifted off from Blue Origin’s launchpad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. It did not blast off like the rockets of old. Accelerometers and gyroscopes fed its position to the guidance system as computers continuously adjusted thrust and steering, making millions of pounds of rocket seem almost to levitate. When the rocket disappeared, it left behind a long, knobby cloud—a strangely beautiful albino Cheeto. Six minutes later, the booster landed a few hundred miles away in the Atlantic Ocean on the drone ship Jacklyn, named for Bezos’s late mother. Everyone went nuts. I didn’t find out for a few hours that the mission had been a dud. One of NG‑3’s engines had failed to produce enough thrust and dropped AST’s satellite in the wrong orbit, too low to be useful. AST had insurance, but the customer doesn’t care if you save money by reusing your booster; it cares that you get the job done. Blue Origin had not. At 12:12 p.m., the day got a little worse: SpaceX announced that it had just landed its Falcon 9 booster for the 600th time. A month later, a New Glenn rocket undergoing a static-fire test caused the largest explosion in the history of Cape Canaveral, badly damaging Blue Origin’s only operational launchpad and temporarily grounding the program. Only two people have the means and ambition to vertically integrate the galaxy, and one of them has the upper hand. In 2025, SpaceX launched 83 percent of the mass sent into orbit—about 10 times more than its nearest competitor, the Chinese government. Starlink’s 11,000-plus satellites account for roughly two-thirds of all active spacecraft orbiting Earth. Limp, at least, knows all of this. He acknowledged that SpaceX is “by far the leader.” But, he said, “there’s so much demand for space right now that if we get to the scale and the execution of SpaceX, the world will be a happy place. And that does not mean Gwynne and Elon have to fail.” The exact size of that demand is debatable. SpaceX and Blue Origin, along with a handful of smaller competitors, provide launch services to other companies and the federal government, but most of the demand comes from their own or affiliated satellite fleets. In finance, this is called captive demand, and it’s generally regarded with suspicion. In commercial space, it’s called vertical integration, and it’s the whole point. This is why the SpaceX prospectus reads like both a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission and a transcript of an investment banker’s weekend on mushrooms. “Our mission,” it states, “is to build the systems and technologies necessary to make life multiplanetary, to understand the true nature of the universe, and to extend the light of consciousness to the stars.” It then arrives at a number for a total addressable market that includes the light of consciousness: $28.5 trillion. It must have been fun to sit in the room as that number got calculated. Musk’s mesmeric power over investors is well-known. Tesla earned just $3.8 billion in 2025 and is somehow one of the world’s dozen most valuable companies. (Caterpillar, which makes backhoes, earned approximately $8.9 billion.) It’s best to read the prospectus not as a ledger but as the blueprint for a future empire: the East India Company of space. The business is a ladder that starts with rocket-launch capability. The next rung up is satellite arrays. This is a much more profitable business—Starlink really does pay for most everything at SpaceX—but it depends on launch capability. The third rung requires a leap of engineering faith: data centers in space. The fourth is the reason to build them—control over an off-world computing economy capable of training and running AI models at a scale that’s hard to achieve on Earth. In January, SpaceX filed a proposal with the FCC to operate up to 1 million data-center satellites in orbit—describing the project, in the filing itself, as the “first step towards becoming a Kardashev II–level civilization.” A Kardashev Type II civilization is one capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its star. Does this sound crazy? If so, technology’s biggest players are eager to break into the asylum. Space offers AI companies abundant solar energy available 24 hours a day, and freedom from the NIMBYism that makes earthbound data centers and power plants so contentious. “Should I make a rocket company?” OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, asked on a podcast in 2025. OpenAI subsequently tried, unsuccessfully, to take over Stoke Space, a reusable-rocket start-up founded by former Blue Origin employees. Alphabet’s Google and the satellite operator Planet intend to launch two prototype satellites in early 2027 to test whether AI chips can operate effectively in orbit. Google and OpenAI do not have their own ladders. Musk does, and he’s already climbed the first two rungs; in August, he posted that SpaceX would put its first satellite data center in orbit by the end of next year. Bezos is in between—he has a ladder; it’s just shorter and shakier. The question is how much the gap matters as the race moves upward, into new areas of engineering and imagination where no one—not even SpaceX—has a lead. In late 2027, Blue Origin plans to deploy TeraWave, a constellation of 5,408 new satellites custom designed to provide data centers and governments with internet up to 6,000 times faster than Amazon’s satellites. New Glenn is expected to place TeraWave into orbit. John Couluris leads Blue Origin’s lunar-permanence team, charged with creating the infrastructure for colonization. “Maybe seven years ago, people wouldn’t have said, ‘Well, we could do data centers on the moon,’ ” Couluris told me. Now he considers it complicated but more and more plausible. The challenges are real—chips fail, cosmic radiation is weird, and maintenance is essentially impossible. But if launch costs continue to drop, they’ll offset the expense. Couluris said Blue Origin is already working on manufacturing solar cells directly from lunar soil. The chips would come from Earth; almost everything else could be made on-site. The destination for all of this potential computing power has only recently become clear. In 2024, I heard rumors about Prometheus, a company whose plans were inscrutable even by the standards of AI start-ups. No one associated with Prometheus would confirm its existence. Given the history of Blue Origin, this should have been a tell. What’s now known is that Prometheus is trying to build something quite different from the generative-AI models that spit out text or code. The most complicated things that humans create—jet engines, drug molecules, semiconductors—live at the intersection of invention and engineering, where physical forces interact in ways that are expensive to model and even more expensive to test. An engineer can sketch a thousand designs; each one still has to survive contact with physics. Prometheus is intended to compress that process—to create an artificial general engineer capable not merely of proposing designs, but, it seems, of simulating, testing, refining, and, eventually, helping manufacture them. The grandest possible outcome is a machine that makes machines. There’s an echo here for Bezos. Neal Stephenson and Blue Origin’s other early employees spent years exploring engineering possibilities in slow motion while the competition raced ahead. An artificial general engineer could compress all of that painstaking discovery into rapid computation: a Neal Stephenson bot. This could be useful to all humankind—and particularly useful to someone trying to build dexterous warehouse robots, cheaper rockets, and data centers on the moon. Whether any of this is possible, and on what timeline, is unknown. Large language models were jump-started by the availability (or theft) of trillions of words; there’s less training data on the physical world. The models also have to understand multiple kinds of physics at once, account for uncertainty, and produce results trustworthy enough to bet hardware and human lives on. Those problems are very expensive to solve. At least for most people. In November 2025, Prometheus’s existence became public, along with the news that it had raised $6.2 billion, the largest chunk of which came from Bezos. He was also named co-CEO, his first operational role since Amazon. Prometheus has since hired 150 people, many from OpenAI and Google DeepMind. Dave told me that Bezos spends his days bouncing between Prometheus and Blue Origin. “But he multitasks very well. Well, he single-tasks in a multitask world very well.” Musk already has his own AI company, xAI, which he merged with SpaceX. His chatbot, Grok, has mostly distinguished itself through creepiness and anti-Semitism, but Musk used $60 billion in stock from the IPO to buy Cursor, an AI-coding assistant that’s one of the fastest-growing software companies. That leaves tens of billions more to spend on the most precious commodity in tech: margin for error. It’s not a coincidence that, a few weeks after the SpaceX IPO, Blue Origin said it had secured $10 billion in outside funding, the first non-Bezos money in the company’s 26-year history. Limp called it a sign of confidence. It was also an acknowledgment of reality: Blue Origin is going to need more money. It has less margin, and more errors. Gary Hershorn / Getty A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket passes over Lower Manhattan in August. SpaceX is winding down Falcon 9, the workhorse rocket that’s served as the West’s space-transportation system, in order to concentrate on Starship (as of this writing, the company was preparing for its 14th test flight—the first to attempt orbit). Other satellite companies have reported trouble buying Falcon launches beyond 2028. Starship will offer significantly more capacity—but SpaceX may use much of that capacity itself: Starlink and the orbital data centers it hopes to build are potentially far more lucrative than carrying other people’s satellites. In other words, the company that solved America’s launch shortage may now be creating another one. This is not just a business problem. It also matters to a sovereign nation that has recently discovered that one of its citizens possesses powers normally reserved for states. All of humanity may learn what it means to have its future built atop someone else’s rocket. In 2022, Ukraine asked Musk to extend Starlink coverage over Crimea so it could carry out military operations. Musk refused. General Mark Milley, then the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and National Security Adviser Sullivan spoke with him about the decision. “And there wasn’t much we could do about that, absent taking some very coercive measures,” Sullivan told me—measures no one wants to take. Three years later, during an X fight with Trump, Musk threatened to immediately decommission SpaceX’s Dragon capsule, the only American vehicle capable of transporting astronauts to and from the International Space Station. Without it, NASA would have had to pay Russia $80 million a seat on Soyuz capsules. A few hours later, Musk backed down. “We absolutely need diversification on this,” Sullivan said. “And what’s challenging is that the most likely pathway to diversification lies through another mercurial billionaire.” That the republic finds itself needing Bezos’s extraordinary concentration of private power to mitigate Musk’s extraordinary concentration of private power is probably not what the Founders had in mind. I asked Senator Mark Kelly, a former astronaut, if he trusted either man completely. He replied, “Kind of a loaded question.” Kelly has met Bezos. His history with Musk dates back to at least 2012, when he joined SpaceX’s human-spaceflight safety-advisory panel, consulting on the Dragon capsule that would eventually make SpaceX indispensable to NASA. After Kelly, who serves on the Armed Services and Intelligence Committees, visited Ukraine in 2025, Musk called him a “traitor” on X. So it goes. But Kelly doesn’t begrudge SpaceX its dominance. “It’s not SpaceX’s fault, right?” Kelly said. “They got ahead. They do it well.” What he wants is for SpaceX to “continue to be a successful company because it is in our national-security interest that that’s the case. I also want to see Blue Origin be successful.” The pragmatist’s position, shared by most of the national-security community, is that one company capable of getting you to space is better than none, and two is better than one. But even if Bezos is the less mercurial billionaire, Blue Origin is not yet a reliable substitute for SpaceX. Andrew Harnik / Getty At the start of Trump’s second term, Elon Musk served as a senior adviser to the president and wielded extraordinary influence. So the government can’t use Blue Origin as leverage. It can threaten to withhold contracts from SpaceX, but, as Trump discovered, Musk will respond by threatening to decommission the only American vehicle capable of reaching the space station. It can nationalize the companies, which would require a political consensus that doesn’t exist and a legal argument that hasn’t been made. Kelly thinks campaign-finance reform would make it harder for the next Musk to buy his way into the center of government, or the next Bezos to buy his way back into its good graces. When I asked which is more likely to happen first—campaign-finance reform or data centers on the moon—Kelly laughed. “I hope it’s campaign-finance reform.” The government is not negotiating from a position of strength, but Bezos and Musk have a shared vulnerability: Both say they would like to go to the moon—for their empires, for glory, and because their youthful love of space has never settled into something more rational. To put it in terms they and the president would all understand, the moon is leverage. If the people trying to bargain with Charles Foster Kane had known about Rosebud, they would have dangled a sled. For all of the stated urgency of the 2016 Trump transition meeting, what’s really happening with America’s return to the moon is only just now coming into view. In February, Musk posted on X that SpaceX had shifted focus from Mars to building a “self-growing city on the Moon.” The SpaceX prospectus has a section called “Establish the lunar economy,” which includes a base supplied by a continuous flow of people and cargo, eventually capable of producing its own water, fuel, power, and manufactured goods. Moontown sounds great, but the engineering details are a kind of truth serum—revealing the distance between what Bezos and Musk say they want and where their priorities actually lie. SpaceX’s Starship cannot get to the moon without stopping for gas. The plan it sold NASA works roughly like this: SpaceX launches a Starship to serve as a fuel depot; then it launches a succession of tanker Starships to fill the depot; then it launches the lunar lander, which gasses up at the depot and departs for the moon. NASA’s Office of Inspector General estimates that at least 15 Starship launches will be needed to deliver all the fuel. No spacecraft has ever transferred ultracold methane and oxygen between vehicles in orbit. In August, SpaceX committed $100 billion to build what Musk called “the biggest launch site on Earth” in Louisiana. This, along with its other facilities, should allow it, eventually, to launch multiple rockets a day. But even if SpaceX can get refueler rockets to the depot before the other rockets run out of gas, Doug Loverro, NASA’s former associate administrator for human exploration and operations, told me he’s skeptical of all the other things Starship has to prove: that it can reach orbit, keep astronauts alive, transfer fuel repeatedly in space, fly to the moon, land, and—crucially, if you’re an astronaut—take off again. His point is not that any single step is impossible. It’s the sheer number of steps that have to work in sequence. “Hurdle No. 1 is let’s get Starship to orbit,” Loverro said. “Which still hasn’t happened yet.” Blue Origin’s route to the moon is complicated too: New Glenn first sends a transporter into low Earth orbit to be refueled. The lander, Blue Moon, launches separately, takes on fuel, and heads toward the moon, while the transporter climbs to a higher orbit for another fill. Near the moon, the two dock for one final transfer. Only then do the astronauts arrive and move into Blue Moon, which they use to descend to the surface and return to their spacecraft. It’s an elaborate chain of rendezvous and refuelings, but the jobs are divided among purpose-built vehicles: New Glenn launches, the transporter carries fuel across deep space, and Blue Moon lands. SpaceX assigns nearly all of those jobs to variants of the same enormous Starship. Saul loeb / AFP / Getty Jeff Bezos unveils Blue Moon, a lunar lander, in Washington, D.C., in 2019. Also, as NASA’s Office of Inspector General has pointed out, Starship’s lander is 171 feet tall—roughly the equivalent of a 14-story building—and its astronauts descend in an elevator that begins 115 feet up. There’s no other way back into the vehicle if the elevator fails. Blue Moon is 52 feet, and its crew walks down a set of stairs that starts six feet off the ground. If you’re curious why, 60 years after Apollo, getting to the moon seems harder, part of the answer is that NASA has 60 years of pent-up expectations. The original astronauts flew in tin cans atop disposable rockets. A sustained presence on the moon will require more mass and more propellant. Most people I spoke with have reached the same conclusion: On this, Blue Origin is ahead. It has completed thermal-vacuum testing on Blue Moon, and, as of August, its structure, propulsion, and avionics were fully assembled; it’s already communicating with NASA’s satellites and deep-space network. Even with the launchpad explosion, Blue Origin still plans to deliver an uncrewed test mission to the moon by early next year. That first flight will be a chance to work out many of Blue Origin’s hardest lunar-specific tasks on a single trip. The crux of the difference is that Blue Origin—the smaller, slower company in need of a win—seems to have built a product to fit the brief, while Musk has built a giant rocket designed for his satellite business and his personal goal of deep-space travel to Mars. Making Starship work for the moon is like adapting a cargo ship to win a yacht race. None of this guarantees that Blue Origin gets to the moon first. “I’m the first to say never count Elon out,” Loverro told me. “He’s a clever guy.” It also doesn’t really solve the mercurial-billionaire problem as much as shift it. But Loverro had a suggestion so simple and clever that it made me laugh out loud. The Apollo missions also sprang from private industry, but NASA divided the work among contractors—Boeing, North American Aviation, IBM, and more. Different companies, different roles, forced into collaboration by NASA. Why not make Starship the refueling station for Blue Moon? SpaceX would have to reconfigure some of its designs, but “it only takes one Starship to fill up a Blue lander. It may take 10 or 15 Starships to fill up a Starship lander. If they work together, they could both get there sooner. “We’re individualistic in the United States,” Loverro continued. “Every man for themselves. But that’s not how we do great things. We do great things because we find the best of everything that we can bring to the table, and then we do it together. That’s what NASA’s job truly is—to organize that team. And they’re failing to do so.” The person responsible for organizing that team is NASA’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, a self-made billionaire who twice flew to space on SpaceX’s Dragon capsule and performed the first private spacewalk. His relationship with Musk complicated his confirmation. On his first day in the job, Isaacman said that whichever lander was ready first would get the mission. He declined an interview request for this story. Isaacman may hold to his winner-take-all position. He may avoid angering two of America’s most powerful men and hope their engineering successes or failures make the decision for him. But the Solomonic solution has a certain appeal: Force Musk and Bezos to work together, and test their willingness to share a win. One small step toward reminding them that the nation is still king. This article appears in the November 2026 print edition with the headline “Choose Your Overlord.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. items.title: Wike asks Amaechi to explain outcome of alleged $10m Rivers fumigation project
items.description: The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has challenged Rotimi Amaechi, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) vice-presidential candidate, to explain the outcome of a $10 million fumigation project reportedly undertaken during his tenure as Rivers State governor. Wike made the call during a media chat on Tuesday while responding to a question on why he had been criticising the former governor. The FCT minister denied targeting Amaechi, saying the former governor should expect scrutiny because of his ambition to become Nigeria’s vice-president. He argued that Amaechi’s aspiration to occupy the country’s second-highest political office made it necessary for Nigerians to examine his record and past decisions. “You can’t just want to run for a position without anybody telling you the past. So, let Nigerians judge if all these things are correct,” Wike said. He challenged Amaechi to account for the fumigation project, recalling that the former governor had promised to rid Rivers State of mosquitoes and malaria. “You told Rivers people that you’re going to fumigate the state so they won’t be suffering from malaria, and you paid 10 million dollars to a company in Cuba. Could you tell Nigerians what is the effect of that fumigation?” he asked. Wike also faulted Amaechi for making allegations against President Bola Tinubu and members of his administration, including describing the president as a thief. The minister said such statements required scrutiny, arguing that allegations against a sitting president could have implications beyond the individual occupying the office. He maintained that Amaechi should be prepared to answer questions about his public record rather than portray himself as an exemplary leader while campaigning for political office. Wike, however, said he had no objection to Amaechi criticising Tinubu, but argued that the former governor should be held accountable for his own claims and actions. The post Wike asks Amaechi to explain outcome of alleged $10m Rivers fumigation project appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Education is critical to Ghana’s future and development – Haruna Iddrisu
items.description: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has underscored the importance of education to Ghana’s development, describing a child’s entry into school as a defining moment in securing their future. Speaking on Joy FM on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, the Tamale South MP said his role as Education Minister offered an opportunity to contribute to the country’s long-term progress. “I believe that the education portfolio is a very important portfolio for the development and the future of the country,” he said. Mr Iddrisu was responding to a question about whether he missed the day-to-day parliamentary politics associated with his previous leadership role. “Oh, not really,” he responded, before explaining the significance he attached to education. “And my honest belief is that the most important single event in life is for a child to step into school, to get educated. And that is where life, in my view, begins. And that’s where, in my view, the future begins to be secured.” He said missing that opportunity could affect an individual’s personal development and ability to contribute to national progress. “If you miss that opportunity, you probably may not get it right, for the most part, even if you want to contribute to your own self-development and the development of the country.” Mr Iddrisu also noted that his ministerial responsibilities had not ended his participation in parliamentary work. “But I’m still a Member of Parliament. I still have an opportunity to be in Parliament to answer questions as a Minister for Education, subject area-specific questions that come up.”

items.title: Fitch pourrait dégrader la note de la France si la dette continue de grimper
items.description: Dans un communique publie le 12 octobre, l'une des trois grandes agences de notation a souligne les risques pesant sur les finances publiques francaises. La perspective reste pour l'instant stable, mais Fitch previent clairement : l'absence de progres substantiels dans la reduction du deficit pourrait entraîner une revision de la perspective a « Negative », puis une baisse de la notation en cas de nouvelle envolee de la dette. Au debut de l'annee 2026, l'agence de notation Moody's affirmait deja douter « du redressement promis par le gouvernement francais » . Un budget 2027 juge insuffisant face a la trajectoire de la dette Le projet de loi de finances presente par le gouvernement « met en evidence la difficulte croissante a reduire le deficit budgetaire et a stabiliser la dette publique dans un contexte de faible croissance, de hausse des charges d'interets et de fragmentation politique persistante », estime Fitch. L'agence reconnaît le caractere ambitieux du texte, mais juge qu'un ajustement nettement plus important serait necessaire pour stabiliser le ratio d'endettement. Sur le reseau social X, le compte specialise dans l'investissement de David Renan met en garde : « Sans redressement budgetaire, la France risque de perdre sa note actuelle… » 🇫🇷 ALERTE FITCH : LA NOTE DE LA FRANCE MENACÉE ! ⚠️ Fitch met en garde contre une possible dégradation de la note A+ de la France : dette en hausse, croissance faible et instabilité politique fragilisent les finances publiques. 👉 Sans redressement budgétaire, la France risque de perdre sa note actuelle … — David Renan (@DavidRenanTrade) October 12, 2026 Le deficit est desormais prevu a 5,4 % du produit interieur brut (PIB) en 2026, au-dela de l'objectif initial de 5 %. Sans mesures supplementaires, il pourrait atteindre 6,4 % en 2027. Fitch calcule qu'un effort cumule d'environ 3,5 % du PIB serait requis pour stabiliser la dette, contre 3 % estimes en août. La charge d'interets, qui ne representait que 0,3 % du PIB l'an dernier, devrait grimper a 0,8 % entre 2026 et 2028. a cela s'ajoute un contexte social tendu qui « rend difficile l'assainissement budgetaire » et cree des pressions pour davantage de depenses. Sur France Inter, le president du directoire d'Euronext Stephane Boujnah estime que le pays n'est pas encore en crise financiere, « mais ce n'est plus impossible [qu'on y arrive] ». La responsable du bureau parisien du journal britannique The Economist Sophie Pedder alerte sur le fait que l'on traite la dette de maniere « un peu abstraite » en France alors qu'il s'agit de l'argent des Francais. “La France n’est pas encore en crise financière, mais ce n’est plus impossible [qu’on y arrive]” Stéphane Boujnah, président du directoire d'Euronext depuis 2015 et Sophie Pedder, cheffe du bureau parisien du journal britannique The Economist, sont les invités de Florence Paracuellos et @Ben_Duhamel ➡️ https://t.co/fLtdA7fJm4 — France Inter (@franceinter) October 13, 2026 Cet avertissement survient juste avant l'ouverture des debats sur le budget 2027 a l'Assemblee nationale, alors que les oppositions ont deja propose d'aggraver le deficit de huit milliards en commission . Une degradation rendrait plus coûteux le financement de l'etat, les investisseurs exigeant des taux plus eleves sur les obligations francaises.

items.title: 'Our future is being robbed': Greta Thunberg joins France student protests
items.description: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined high school pupils campaigning for better learning conditions in France on Tuesday ahead of fresh nationwide demonstrations , with authorities and participants wary of further violence. The 23-year-old, who became famous as a teen for school strikes to demand action on climate change, stood among pupils demonstrating outside a school at the heart of the movement in the capital’s largest suburb of Saint-Denis. Thunberg arrived at the Paul Eluard high school, as lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect teens after numerous allegations of police brutality. “Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us,” Thunberg told AFP . The mobilisation , which is backed by unions and the far-left opposition France Unbowed party, was to include a midday march through Paris, along with marches in other cities. “They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them,” university student union l’Union etudiante wrote on X. More than 70,000 people took to the streets last Thursday in the last major event of a movement that sprung up in late September. French authorities had been hoping that the protests would start to ease ahead of half-term holidays. “We should be at around… 200 schools closed, which is fewer than last week,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on France Inter on Tuesday morning, adding some near protest routes were closing to avoid damage. In the Paris region, teenagers had blockaded the entrances to several schools before dawn. In the southern city of Marseille, students slowly pushed dumpsters on wheels in front of their high school. ‘Aren’t being heard’ French students say they are determined to press the government to address the problems of too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances. The protests since last month have seen teenagers pile up dumpsters and light security barriers outside hundreds of France’s 3,700 lycees for students mostly aged 15 to 18. They have mostly been peaceful, but seen clashes occasionally break out with police. The education ministry said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, in relation to the protests. “Students aren’t being heard enough… not their proposals to authorities and elected officials,” a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, said on Monday. He added that the protesters — many of whom were minors — were “disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement”. Protesters hold placards and banners during a demonstration of high-school students in Lyon, southeastern France on October 13, 2026, as part of a nationwide high school mobilisation. — AFP Thousands of arrests Authorities said fireworks fired through a tube injured two school workers in Reims, one school worker in a Paris suburb and a police officer outside a school in Marseille. Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students were to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living . Naila, a 17-year-old student in the city of Rennes who said she would participate in Tuesday’s demonstration, hoped it would “converge” with the wider one on Saturday. President Emmanuel Macron, speaking to reporters at a car show on Monday, urged restraint from protesters. “These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said just months before elections to replace him. More than 6,800 people — largely minors — have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests, according to the justice ministry. Police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators. This photograph shows a banner which reads as ’Macron, You break scholl! — AFP After last week’s nationwide demonstrations, the government promised some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools. The education minister said on Tuesday that 35 per cent had already been assigned. High school students are demanding a 10 billion-euro ($11bn) boost for lycees (upper-level secondary schools in France).

items.title: Patrimoine Gala : la culture sénégalaise rayonne de l’UNESCO à la Tour Eiffel
items.description: De l’UNESCO à la Tour Eiffel, en passant par Montreuil, la troisième édition du Patrimoine Gala a mis en lumière les traditions, les coiffures et les costumes sénégalais à Paris, du 30 septembre au 10 octobre 2026. Initiée par Papis Niang et produite par Art Bi Management, cette édition s’est déroulée sous le thème « Nagn Déllu Saaraba ». Le patrimoine culturel sénégalais s’est invité dans la capitale française. Du siège de l’UNESCO aux rues de Paris, en passant par l’Espace Royal de Montreuil, la troisième édition du Patrimoine Gala a célébré les traditions et l’identité sénégalaises. Organisée du 30 septembre au 10 octobre 2026, cette initiative entend rapprocher les peuples par la culture et renforcer les liens entre la diaspora et ses racines. Le premier temps fort s’est tenu le 30 septembre au siège de l’UNESCO, à l’occasion de l’événement « L’UNESCO au cœur des JOJ Dakar 2026 », organisé à l’initiative de la Délégation permanente du Sénégal, en partenariat avec la Grèce, à un mois des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse. La rencontre s’est déroulée en présence du directeur général de l’UNESCO, Khaled El Enany, de la ministre de la Jeunesse et des Sports du Sénégal, Djirèye Clotilde Coly, ainsi que de l’ambassadeur et délégué permanent du Sénégal auprès de l’UNESCO, Pierre Maad Faye, et de plusieurs délégations internationales. Le message porté par cette rencontre se résumait en ces termes : « Saaraba rassemble, l’Afrique accueille, Dakar célèbre. » Le 9 octobre, l’Espace Royal de Montreuil a accueilli « Ëttu Saaraba », une soirée consacrée à la culture traditionnelle sénégalaise. Animée par Fatou Guéweul Diouf et Tarba Mbaye, elle a réuni plusieurs personnalités, dont l’ambassadeur du Sénégal en France, Baye Moctar Diop, et Pierre Maad Faye, ainsi que des maires, des adjoints au maire et des élus locaux. Le lendemain, les rues de Paris ont servi de décor à la balade « Tenkam Tenkam ». À proximité de la Tour Eiffel, des figures symboliques de l’histoire et de l’imaginaire sénégalais ont été mises à l’honneur, notamment Lat Dior Ngoné Latyr et Maam Penda Mbaye, aux côtés d’Assia Yatabaré, présentée comme la Reine de l’Or. Cette séquence a également été marquée par la présentation officielle de la Reine Saaraba par El Hadj Bécaye Mbaye. Selon le communiqué, cette figure emblématique aura pour mission de promouvoir « la reconnexion aux racines, la transmission du patrimoine, le dialogue interculturel, la paix et l’égalité humaine ». La culture comme trait d’union À travers le Patrimoine Gala, l’initiateur, Papis Niang, défend une vision de la culture comme levier de transmission et de rapprochement entre les peuples. « Un peuple qui connaît son patrimoine connaît une partie de sa force », souligne-t-il. Pour les organisateurs, la rencontre entre les cultures ne doit pas se faire au détriment des identités. À Paris, le rendez-vous a ainsi mis en avant le patrimoine sénégalais comme un langage universel, capable de dépasser les frontières, de relier les générations et de rapprocher la diaspora de ses origines. Cette ambition doit se prolonger avec SAARABA WORLD, un univers consacré au patrimoine, à la création et au dialogue interculturel. Le projet entend offrir aux artistes, aux artisans et aux jeunes talents des opportunités de visibilité et de collaboration. Les organisateurs souhaitent faire du Patrimoine Gala un rendez-vous annuel, international et durable. Après cette étape parisienne, le Patrimoine Gala prévoit de poursuivre son déploiement à l’international. Le prochain rendez-vous est annoncé en 2027, en Angleterre et aux États-Unis, avec l’ambition de renforcer les échanges avec les diasporas et de donner davantage d’ampleur à SAARABA WORLD. A.N

items.title: 91 microentreprises sur 100 restent actives grâce au projet IMPACT-BF
items.description: À Tenkodogo, Bittou, Koupéla et Pouytenga, un projet d’entrepreneuriat inclusif aide des personnes affectées par la crise, dont des personnes en situation de handicap, à retrouver leur autonomie financière. Au 30 septembre 2026, 91 des 100 activités génératrices de revenus (AGR) lancées étaient toujours actives. Au Burkina Faso, les autorités encouragent les organisations et les projets humanitaires à ne pas se limiter à l’urgence, mais à miser sur le relèvement des communautés. Cette orientation vise à renforcer la résilience des populations affectées par la crise et à restaurer durablement leurs moyens d’existence. Le projet « Mesures d’inclusion pour les personnes affectées par la crise dans les zones ciblées au Burkina Faso » (IMPACT-BF) s’inscrit dans cette dynamique. Un consortium au service du relèvement Le projet est porté par Light for the World, la Croix-Rouge burkinabè (CRBF) et l’Association d’appui et d’éveil Pugsada (ADEP), avec le soutien financier de la Coopération autrichienne (ADA). Il place l’inclusion du handicap et l’équité de genre au cœur de son action, afin que le relèvement profite à toutes les composantes de la communauté. Les bénéficiaires ont été identifiés avec les services provinciaux de l’action humanitaire et les organisations de personnes handicapées, en cohérence avec les structures locales. Au total, 100 personnes issues des communautés déplacées et des communautés hôtes ont suivi un parcours de formation en entrepreneuriat, en gestion financière et dans des métiers porteurs. Des activités ancrées dans les réalités locales Les activités retenues valorisent les opportunités économiques de chaque zone : aviculture, embouche ovine et porcine, mécanique moto, petit commerce, saponification, tissage et transformation agroalimentaire. Ce choix contribue à dynamiser les économies locales et à créer de la valeur au sein même des communautés. Les bénéficiaires ont aussi élaboré leurs plans d’affaires et renforcé leurs compétences en gestion financière, en marketing, en épargne, en accès au microcrédit et en réinvestissement. Des fonds de roulement, des équipements et des intrants ont ensuite permis le démarrage de leurs entreprises. Un taux de maintien de 91 % Selon l’évaluation arrêtée au 30 septembre 2026, 91 activités sur 100 restent actives : 23 à Tenkodogo, 23 à Bittou, 23 à Koupéla et 22 à Pouytenga, soit un taux de maintien en activité de 91 %. Ce chiffre montre une continuité économique encourageante, mais il ne suffit pas à mesurer la rentabilité ni la pérennité des entreprises. Les mobilités géographiques, les interruptions temporaires et les abandons relevés rappellent la nécessité d’un accompagnement adapté aux réalités de chaque bénéficiaire. Consolider pour inscrire le relèvement dans la durée L’enjeu est désormais de pérenniser ces résultats. Cela passe par un suivi régulier, un meilleur accès aux débouchés et le renforcement des capacités de réinvestissement des bénéficiaires. La poursuite de la collaboration avec les services de l’État et les acteurs locaux demeure déterminante pour y parvenir. Avec IMPACT-BF, l’objectif est de permettre à des personnes vulnérables de passer du statut de bénéficiaires de l’aide à celui d’acteurs de leur propre reconstruction économique, en phase avec la volonté affichée de privilégier le relèvement communautaire. Correspondance particulière Faso7 L’article 91 microentreprises sur 100 restent actives grâce au projet IMPACT-BF est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Protesting military veterans demand fair pension adjustment, block board entrance
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi Scores of retired military veterans on Tuesday blocked the entrance to the Military Pensions Board office in Dutse Alhaji, Abuja, over concerns about the formula adopted for adjusting the increment in their pensions. The veterans, as early as 8 a.m., barricaded the entrance with canopies and chairs, while armed soldiers prevented them from entering the premises. The action comes weeks after military retirees protested at the Ministry of Defence in September, demanding an increase in their pensions following salary adjustments for serving military personnel. Recall that the Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa Rtd, had in August promised that the retirees would receive an increase in their pensions in October following President Tinubu’s approval for an increase in salaries of armed forces personnel. Speaking in an interview, one of the coordinators of the Veterans Association of Nigeria, Lt Col Innocent Azubike Rtd, alleged that the board had adopted a pension adjustment formula that allegedly short-changed some retirees. Azubike said the planned protest followed growing dissatisfaction among veterans over the implementation of consequential adjustments to their pensions. The veterans’ concerns centre on the formula used to calculate the adjustments, which they believe has failed to adequately reflect the salary increases granted to serving military personnel. items.title: PAM et Koutla, un attelage à l'heure de gouverner
items.description: Au terme de deux rounds de consultations, la Cheffe du gouvernement désignée, Fatima-Zahra Mansouri, a tranché. Le Parti authenticité et modernité (PAM), arrivé en tête des législatives du 23 septembre, formera la prochaine majorité avec l'Istiqlal (PI), l’Union socialiste des forces populaires (USFP) et le Parti du Progrès et du Socialisme (PPS). L'accord a été officialisé ce lundi 12 octobre par un communiqué conjoint des quatre formations. La coalition compte 207 députés sur 395 à la Chambre des représentants, soit neuf sièges au-dessus du seuil de la majorité absolue. Cette configuration donne au PAM le rôle de force centrale, tout en associant trois formations qui constituent le cœur de l'ancienne Koutla. Selon le communiqué, le choix repose sur la volonté de constituer une majorité « politique », cohérente dans ses orientations et capable de relever les défis auxquels le Maroc est confronté, sur le plan intérieur comme international. L'objectif affiché est de disposer d'une majorité à même d'accompagner les orientations royales en matière de construction démocratique, de bonne gouvernance, de justice sociale, d'équité territoriale et de renforcement des capacités productives de l'économie nationale. L'accord ouvre désormais la phase de composition de l'Exécutif. Les quatre partis doivent proposer des noms de ministres répondant à plusieurs critères : compétence, sens politique, intégrité et probité. Fatima-Zahra Mansouri, qui affiche la volonté d'avancer rapidement, leur demande également de travailler à l'élaboration du programme gouvernemental. Ce que révèle cette nouvelle majorité Dans un commentaire livré à Hespress FR , Rachid Lazrak, professeur de sciences politiques et de droit constitutionnel et directeur du Centre nord-africain d'études, de recherches et d'évaluation des politiques publiques, indique que la constitution de cette nouvelle majorité gouvernementale marque une étape importante dans la recomposition du paysage politique marocain. Au-delà de l'accord entre quatre formations politiques, explique-t-il, elle traduit une volonté de construire une coalition autour d'un projet politique commun, plutôt que sur la seule logique arithmétique des alliances parlementaires. Le premier enseignement, souligne le professeur de sciences politiques, réside dans la configuration politique de cette majorité. Le Parti authenticité et modernité, arrivé en tête des élections législatives, s'allie aux trois composantes historiques de la Koutla démocratique : l'Istiqlal, l'Union socialiste des forces populaires et le Parti du progrès et du socialisme. Cette configuration, note Lazarak, présente une forte portée symbolique et politique. Elle consacre le rapprochement de formations issues de trajectoires historiques différentes, autour d'une ambition affichée de réforme, de justice sociale et de développement territorial équilibré. Le deuxième enseignement, fait-il observer, concerne la nature de cette majorité. Avec 207 sièges, elle dispose de la majorité absolue à la Chambre des représentants, mais sa marge parlementaire demeure relativement étroite. Sa stabilité, affirme-t-il, dépendra donc moins du nombre de partis qui la composent que de leur capacité à maintenir une discipline collective, à dépasser leurs divergences et à traduire leurs engagements en politiques publiques cohérentes. Enfin, relève Rachid Lazrak, cette nouvelle étape intervient dans un contexte politique inédit, marqué par la désignation, pour la première fois dans l'histoire du Maroc, d'une femme à la tête du gouvernement. Cette avancée symbolique importante, ajoute-t-il, devra s'accompagner d'une nouvelle dynamique dans la gouvernance publique et dans la réponse aux attentes sociales. En définitive, la véritable épreuve de cette majorité ne sera pas, de l'avis de l'universitaire, sa constitution, mais sa capacité à gouverner ensemble et à produire des résultats tangibles. Sa crédibilité, poursuit-il, se mesurera notamment à la qualité de son programme gouvernemental, à la cohérence de son équipe et à sa capacité à répondre aux préoccupations des citoyens, particulièrement en matière d’emploi, de santé, d'éducation, de pouvoir d'achat et de réduction des disparités territoriales. The post PAM et Koutla, un attelage à l'heure de gouverner appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: When the Laboratory Comes to You: How SYNLAB’s Home Sample Collection Experience Is Balancing Convenience with Quality
items.description: From traffic and waiting rooms to doorstep diagnostics, SYNLAB’s home sample collection service is making laboratory testing more convenient, while keeping the focus on quality and accuracy. For many Nigerians, getting a laboratory test begins with a journey. There is the traffic, the time away from work, the waiting room and, sometimes, the decision to postpone the test altogether because the day is simply too busy. However, Nigerians have another option, called home sample collection; where a trained healthcare professional comes to the patient’s home to collect the required sample and takes it to the laboratory for processing. At SYNLAB Nigeria , this service is designed around the simple idea that healthcare should be accessible without unnecessary disruption to people’s lives. Instead of patients travelling to a diagnostic Centre simply to have a sample collected, SYNLAB brings the collection service to them. While offering convenience makes for quick access to care, it raises an important question: Can a test collected at home be as reliable as one collected inside a diagnostic Centre? The answer to this lies in the process behind the testing, not the location of the sample collection. The Location Is Not What Determines Accuracy Laboratory accuracy depends on several stages of the testing process. These include how the patient prepares for the test, how the sample is collected, how it is identified and labelled, how it is transported and stored, and how it is eventually processed in the laboratory. None of these factors inherently requires the patient to be inside a diagnostic Centre. SYNLAB ‘s approach to home sample collection follows the same fundamental standards applied to samples collected at its service centres. A trained and certified phlebotomist collects the sample using appropriate sterile equipment and established procedures before it enters the laboratory testing process. The important distinction, therefore, is between home collection and poorly managed collection. A sample collected at home is not automatically less reliable. But a home collection service that lacks trained personnel, proper identification procedures or appropriate transportation and handling processes can create risks. One of the most important considerations is what happens to the sample after collection. Some laboratory tests are sensitive to time and temperature. If a sample is not transported appropriately, its integrity can potentially be affected. This makes transportation and logistics a critical part of SYNLAB’s home collection process. The competence of the person collecting the sample is equally important. SYNLAB uses trained and certified phlebotomists for its home collections, applying appropriate collection techniques and sample identification procedures. Patient preparation also matters. Some tests require fasting, while other results may be influenced by hydration, medication or the timing of sample collection. SYNLAB therefore provides patients with the relevant preparation instructions when they book their tests. Correct identification and labelling are another essential safeguard. From the point of collection, the sample needs to remain correctly linked to the patient throughout the testing process. What Happens When You Book a SYNLAB Home Test? For patients using home collection for the first time, the process is relatively straightforward. It begins with booking the required test and selecting a suitable appointment time. Depending on the patient’s location and the test required, SYNLAB home collection appointments may be available for same-day or next-day service. Bookings can be made through the SYNLAB Nigeria website or by contacting its Customer Support team. At the agreed time, a trained SYNLAB phlebotomist visits the patient’s home with the necessary collection equipment. The patient’s identity is verified, the collection process is explained, and the sample is taken using appropriate clinical procedures. For a blood test, the actual collection is essentially the same procedure a patient would experience at a SYNLAB service Centre. The difference is that the patient does not have to make the journey. From the Home to the Laboratory A home sample is not simply collected and left to make its way to the laboratory without controls. Where specific temperature or handling conditions are required, these form part of the transportation process. SYNLAB’s logistics process is designed to protect sample integrity between collection and laboratory processing. Once the sample reaches the laboratory, it is processed using the appropriate equipment, protocols and quality checks. This is an important part of understanding home testing. The location where the sample is collected may change, but the laboratory where the sample is analyzed does not have to. What Happens to the Results? Once testing is completed, SYNLAB makes results available digitally through its Path Provider result delivery portal. Patients can also receive status notifications through SMS or WhatsApp, helping them stay informed throughout the process. Turnaround time varies depending on the test. Some results may be available within hours, while others require longer processing. This digital component also removes another potential inconvenience: having to return to a diagnostic Centre simply to collect a paper report. An added service of result review by a Pathologist helps the patient or customer understand the next steps when they receive the result. Who Can Benefit from Home Testing? The appeal of home sample collection goes beyond convenience. For people who require regular laboratory monitoring, eliminating the need to repeatedly travel to a diagnostic centre may make it easier to maintain their testing routine. For older adults, particularly those who may find traffic, mobility or prolonged waiting difficult, home collection can remove a significant barrier. For busy professionals and entrepreneurs, it offers another way to fit healthcare into demanding schedules. It can also be useful for families who need several members tested without making multiple trips to a diagnostic centre. For SYNLAB, this is where home collection becomes more than a convenience service. It becomes another way of making diagnostic testing fit into the realities of people’s lives. As healthcare becomes increasingly patient-centred, convenience is becoming an important part of the healthcare experience. Yet convenience does not replace clinical quality. Patients considering home testing should therefore ask several questions: Is the laboratory appropriately accredited? Are the people collecting samples trained and qualified? How are samples transported? Are appropriate handling and identification procedures followed? How and when will results be delivered? These questions help shift the conversation away from whether testing happens at home and towards what matters more: the quality and integrity of the process. SYNLAB’s home collection service is built around maintaining the established diagnostic process while removing some of the logistical burden associated with visiting a diagnostic centre. The laboratory does not necessarily have to be a place the patient travels to; it can be a service that comes to the patient. For Nigerians balancing work, family, traffic and healthcare, that change may be just as significant as the test itself. About SYNLAB SYNLAB Nigeria is a member of the SYNLAB group, with presence in over 20 countries. The organization has over 40 active locations across Nigeria and has been ISO 15189 certified since 2006. SYNLAB Group is the leader in medical diagnostic services and specialty testing in Europe. The Group offers a full range of innovative and reliable medical diagnostics to patients, practicing doctors, hospitals and clinics, governments and corporates. Providing the leading level of service within the industry, SYNLAB is the partner of choice for routine and specialty diagnostics in human and veterinary medicine. The Group continuously innovates medical diagnostic services for the benefit of patients and customers. SYNLAB holds leading positions in most markets, regularly reinforcing the strength of its network through a proven acquisition strategy. items.description: Le Maroc a parfaitement lancé sa campagne à la CAN de futsal 2026 en dominant l’Algérie (4-0), lundi 12 octobre à Rabat. Satisfait de la prestation de ses joueurs, le sélectionneur national Hicham Dguig entend désormais poursuivre sur cette dynamique et atteindre les demi-finales, tout en corrigeant certaines lacunes dans la finition. Les Lions de l’Atlas de futsal ont réussi leur entrée en lice à la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2026. Opposée à l’Algérie lors de la première journée du groupe A, la sélection marocaine s’est imposée sur le score de 4 à 0, lundi soir à Rabat. À l’issue de la rencontre, le sélectionneur national Hicham Dguig a dressé un bilan globalement positif de cette victoire, tout en soulignant les marges de progression de son équipe. Malgré plusieurs occasions manquées, le technicien estime que ses joueurs ont livré une prestation encourageante pour la suite de la compétition. Cette confrontation avait également une dimension particulière, le match revêtant un caractère de derby. Pour Hicham Dguig, cette rencontre représentait aussi une première occasion de retrouver directement le public marocain dans une compétition continentale. Le sélectionneur a notamment souhaité donner du temps de jeu à l’ensemble de ses joueurs afin de leur permettre de prendre leurs marques dans le tournoi. L’objectif des demi-finales en ligne de mire Après ce premier succès, Hicham Dguig préfère avancer étape par étape. La priorité est désormais de décrocher une place dans le dernier carré avant de se projeter sur les échéances suivantes. Le sélectionneur a également relevé les difficultés rencontrées face à une équipe algérienne qui a privilégié une approche défensive pour limiter les dégâts. Ce dispositif a parfois compliqué les offensives marocaines, malgré une domination matérialisée par quatre buts. Pour le technicien marocain, le score aurait même pu être plus large au regard des occasions créées. La capacité à mieux convertir ces opportunités constituera ainsi l’un des principaux axes de travail avant les prochaines rencontres. La finition, un chantier prioritaire Au-delà du résultat, Hicham Dguig souhaite retrouver toute l’énergie et la vivacité qui ont caractérisé les performances de son groupe par le passé. Le staff technique entend notamment travailler sur les détails qui font la différence dans les derniers mètres, en particulier dans les situations proches du but. Cette victoire offre néanmoins une première base positive aux Lions de l’Atlas, qui devront confirmer leur niveau lors des prochaines journées de la phase de groupes. L’ambition est claire : poursuivre leur parcours avec régularité et atteindre les demi-finales avant d’envisager la suite de la compétition.
