items.title: Assemblies of God requires pastors to resign before entering partisan politics – Rev. Wengam
items.description: The Assemblies of God, Ghana, requires pastors seeking to pursue active partisan politics to step down from their ministerial positions, citing provisions in the church’s constitution and code of conduct designed to protect its unity. The church’s General Superintendent, Rev. Stephen Yenusom Wengam, explained that the rule applies to pastors who intend to contest political party primaries or otherwise pursue active partisan political roles. He said the policy allows worshippers with different political affiliations to remain united in their faith without their political differences creating divisions within congregations. Speaking on Channel One TV on Monday, October 12, Rev. Wengam said the requirement was consistent with the church’s global practice, although other denominations might permit their ministers to engage in partisan politics. “Assemblies of God, it can’t happen. You must resign as the pastor of the church,” he said, adding that the rule was enforced during the 2024 election period when two pastors under his leadership resigned after contesting party primaries. He maintained that the restriction did not prevent individuals from pursuing political ambitions but required them to relinquish their pastoral responsibilities before doing so. “It’s a calling, but we are saying that lay down your tools as a pastor. And then pursue your calling,” he added. Rev. Wengam’s comments come ahead of the 2026 World Assemblies of God Congress, scheduled to take place in Ghana from October 14 to 16. The gathering is expected to bring together church leaders from across the world and will be the first time the congress is held on the African continent.

items.title: Pakistan condemns Israeli actions in Syria, calls for withdrawal
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan has condemned continued Israeli military actions in Syria, calling for Israel’s withdrawal from all occupied Syrian territory and full respect for the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement. Speaking at a UN Security Council briefing on the humanitarian and political situation in Syria on Monday evening, Pakistan’s Acting Permanent Representative, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, said Israeli actions violated international law and Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, undermining prospects for regional peace and stability. He reaffirmed that the occupied Syrian Golan remained Syrian territory under international law and relevant UN Security Council resolutions, including resolutions 338 and 497. Ambassador Jadoon also reiterated Pakistan’s support for Syria’s political transition, national reconciliation and economic recovery, stressing the importance of preserving the country’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity. Welcoming renewed diplomatic engagement and efforts to restore national institutions, he expressed optimism about Syria’s future. He backed the Syrian government’s efforts towards an inclusive political transition and welcomed progress in engagement with the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). He called for outstanding challenges, including the situation in Suweida, to be addressed through dialogue and peaceful engagement, with full respect for Syria’s unity and territorial integrity. Emphasising the need for sustained international support, Ambassador Jadoon said reconstruction, economic revival and continued humanitarian assistance were essential to meeting the needs of the Syrian people. He noted that sanctions relief, increased investment and stronger regional and international economic partnerships could provide fresh impetus to Syria’s recovery. The Pakistani envoy also stressed the need for continued vigilance against Daesh and other terrorist groups, including foreign terrorist fighters. He expressed support for Syria’s efforts to strengthen its security and national institutions. Reaffirming the longstanding ties between Pakistan and Syria, Ambassador Jadoon said Islamabad would remain a steadfast friend and partner, committed to strengthening bilateral relations and advancing peace, stability and prosperity for the Syrian people. Last month, a UN commission investigating Syria expressed alarm over Israel’s military activity inside Syrian territory, warning that some actions, including the detention of civilians, could amount to war crimes. In August, eight Israeli airstrikes hit an airbase in northwestern Syria, Syrian state media reported, in what the US envoy for the region called an “unnecessary escalation”. In the months after Assad was toppled, Israel seized ground in southwestern Syria and struck much of the Syrian military’s heavy weapons and equipment, as Israeli officials expressed alarm over the background of Syria’s new rulers.

items.title: Ghana targets 20% annual reduction in maternal deaths – Health Minister
items.description: The Minister of Health, Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, says Ghana is targeting a 20 per cent annual reduction in maternal deaths as part of renewed efforts to improve maternal healthcare and prevent avoidable deaths among pregnant women and new mothers. He said the target reflects the government’s commitment to strengthening maternal health services and ensuring women have access to timely, quality and effective medical care throughout pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period. Mr Akandoh made the disclosure while addressing global health leaders at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany, where he outlined Ghana’s interventions to improve maternal health outcomes. He explained that the government’s commitment to reducing maternal mortality had informed the launch of the Presidential Initiative on Maternal Health Emergency Response (PRIMER), which seeks to strengthen the country’s response to emergencies threatening the lives of pregnant women and mothers. “We recognise that financing alone will not save mothers. It takes political leadership, it takes functioning health systems and it takes accountability for results. That is why under President John Dramani Mahama, we have launched the Presidential Initiative on Maternal Health Emergency Response. Our ambition is clear: to reduce maternal deaths by 20 percent annually,” he said. Mr Akandoh stressed that reducing maternal mortality required more than financial investment, emphasising the need for strong political leadership, functional healthcare systems and accountability for results. The Presidential Initiative on Maternal Health Emergency Response was officially launched on September 16, 2026, by Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang. The initiative is expected to support Ghana’s efforts to improve maternal health outcomes by strengthening emergency responses and ensuring pregnant women and mothers receive timely and appropriate medical care. The 20 per cent annual reduction target forms part of the government’s broader efforts to improve maternal healthcare and prevent deaths that could be avoided through effective interventions and access to quality health services.

items.title: Cyber attacks in Africa grow faster than global rate, report finds
items.description: Nearly 70,000 cyber events were recorded across the continent in 2025, with financial services, technology and public institutions among the main targets. Cyber attacks in Africa increased by 421.4% between 2016 and 2025, outpacing the global increase of 307.3%, according to a new report examining the security risks facing the continent’s expanding digital economy. The figures indicate that if Africa recorded 100 cyberattacks in 2016, the equivalent figure would have risen to about 521 by 2025. Globally, an equivalent starting figure of 100 would have increased to about 407. In other words, the African figure grew to more than five times its 2016 level over nine years, while the global figure rose to just over four times its starting level. The comparison illustrates the faster growth in observed cyber activity in Africa, although the figures do not establish that every African country experienced the same increase or that attacks rose at a constant rate throughout the period. The Africa Cybersecurity Whitepaper: Africa’s Digital Defense Race says 69,236 cyber events targeting African organisations were observed in 2025, equivalent to approximately one recorded event every eight minutes. The report draws on Mastercard Cyber Insights, industry research, law-enforcement intelligence and interviews with cybersecurity experts to examine the threats confronting Africa’s digital infrastructure and the measures needed to strengthen its defences. It focuses on South Africa, Nigeria, Morocco and Kenya, which together accounted for 54.7% of the cyber events observed across Africa in 2025. The findings come as digital payments, financial technology, e-commerce, mobile connectivity and online public services continue to expand, increasing the importance of securing the systems that support businesses, governments and consumers. Financial services and public institutions among key targets Technology companies, public-sector institutions and financial services organisations accounted for 44% of observed cyber threat activity across Africa, the report says. These sectors support essential digital services, including financial transactions, business operations and government services, making their systems important targets for cybercriminals. The report also points to the increasingly organised nature of cybercrime. More than 60% of attributed cyber events were linked to black-hat hackers and organised cybercriminal groups. Black-hat hackers are individuals or groups who use their technical skills to gain unauthorised access to computer systems, steal information, disrupt services or make money illegally. The report examines the methods used by cyber attackers, the industries and digital assets they target, and the state of cybersecurity regulation, governance and national preparedness. Africa’s expanding digital economy is creating new opportunities for businesses and consumers, but it is also increasing the need to protect online transactions, personal information and critical infrastructure. The report projects that the continent’s digital payments market could reach $1.5 trillion by 2030, while its artificial intelligence economy could grow to $16.5 billion by the end of the decade. As more economic activity moves online, weaknesses in digital security can expose organisations to fraud, service disruptions and unauthorised access to sensitive information. The report warns that cybercrime can undermine public confidence in digital services, increase operating costs and slow innovation. Small and medium-sized enterprises may also face risks as they adopt digital tools but lack the resources or specialist personnel available to larger organisations. Governments and financial institutions face similar challenges in protecting the systems on which public services and financial transactions depend. Shortage of cybersecurity professionals A shortage of skilled cybersecurity workers is another challenge identified by the report. Africa has approximately 200,000 unfilled cybersecurity positions, representing a 23% workforce gap, according to the findings. The shortage raises concerns about whether organisations have enough trained personnel to identify vulnerabilities, monitor suspicious activity, investigate incidents and respond to attacks. Strengthening the workforce will require investment in cybersecurity education, professional training and the development of skills needed to protect increasingly complex digital systems. The report also examines cybersecurity regulation and governance, as well as differences in national readiness across the four countries studied. The whitepaper identifies four priority actions to improve cyber resilience across the continent, although the provided summary does not specify them individually. Its broader findings point to the need for stronger protection of critical digital infrastructure, improved preparedness for cyber incidents, effective governance and investment in cybersecurity skills. The report argues that cybersecurity must remain a strategic concern as African economies become more dependent on digital services. The scale of observed cyber activity, the concentration of threats in key economic sectors and the shortage of skilled professionals highlight the challenges facing organisations seeking to protect their systems. For African countries expanding digital payments, online public services and technology-driven businesses, the task is to ensure that security measures keep pace with the growth of the digital economy.

items.title: COP 31 à Antalya, un test pour le multilatéralisme climatique : enjeux pour l’Algérie
items.description: La COP 31 se tiendra du 9 au 20 novembre 2026 à Antalya en Turquie, sur fond de tensions géopolitiques, de crise énergétique et de désaccords persistants sur la réduction des émissions. À Belém, en 2025, la COP 30 n'a pas permis d'inscrire une référence explicite aux énergies fossiles dans le texte final. Antalya devra relancer les discussions sur la transition énergétique . La Turquie accueille la conférence, en assure la présidence et pilote l'Agenda d'action. L'Australie dirige les négociations officielles. Ce partage des responsabilités résulte d'un désaccord prolongé entre les deux pays. La réunion préparatoire aux Fidji a renforcé la visibilité des priorités des petits États insulaires du Pacifique. La Turquie mise sur la mise en œuvre de la COP 31 Ankara veut faire de la COP 31 une « COP de la mise en œuvre », centrée sur les engagements existants, le financement et les énergies propres. La feuille de route de Bakou à Belém vise à mobiliser 1.300 milliards de dollars par an d'ici 2035 pour l'action climatique dans les pays en développement. Le défi consiste à transformer cet objectif en financements accessibles et prévisibles. Murat Kurum, président de la COP 31, défend l'économie circulaire, le programme Zéro Déchet, la lutte contre la déforestation et un objectif mondial d'électrification de 35 % d'ici 2035. Ankara privilégie une diversification progressive plutôt qu'une sortie générale des combustibles fossiles. Cette position lui permet de se présenter en intermédiaire entre pays développés et pays en développement. L'Australie face à ses contradictions Canberra veut poursuivre les négociations sur la sortie du charbon, du pétrole et du gaz. L'Australie reste pourtant l'un des principaux exportateurs mondiaux de combustibles fossiles. Sa crédibilité dépendra de sa capacité à concilier ses engagements climatiques avec ses intérêts énergétiques nationaux. Une ambition collective insuffisante Les États-Unis, la Chine, l'Inde et la Russie défendent des intérêts divergents qui freinent l'ambition climatique collective. Antalya devra favoriser de nouvelles contributions nationales, renforcer les mécanismes de suivi et accélérer l'application des engagements existants. L'adaptation, source de tensions Nord-Sud Les pays vulnérables réclament des financements supplémentaires pour l'adaptation et les pertes et préjudices. Les besoins d'adaptation des pays en développement atteignent plusieurs centaines de milliards de dollars par an. Le fonds pour les pertes et préjudices n'a recueilli qu'environ 800 millions de dollars de promesses, selon les estimations antérieures. Le retrait américain du Fonds vert pour le climat et de la Convention-cadre des Nations unies sur les changements climatiques fragilise la coopération internationale. L'Afrique estime ses besoins climatiques à 2.800 milliards de dollars pour 2020-2030, avec un déficit de 2.500 milliards. Elle réclame qu'au moins la moitié des financements climatiques soit consacrée à l'adaptation. Les petits États insulaires demandent des moyens face à la montée des eaux, à l'érosion côtière et au blanchissement des coraux. Aux Tuvalu, archipel d'environ 10.600 habitants, la submersion menace la continuité territoriale. Les pays du Pacifique placent les océans, le financement et l'objectif de 1,5 °C au cœur des négociations. Combustibles fossiles : les lignes de fracture L'Arabie saoudite s'oppose aux feuilles de route internationales imposant une sortie du pétrole et du gaz. Elle défend la souveraineté énergétique et refuse les trajectoires contraignantes sans consensus. La Russie rejette également les feuilles de route qu'elle estime imposées sans accord collectif. Moscou défend le rôle du gaz naturel dans la sécurité énergétique et la transition. La Chine invoque les responsabilités communes, mais différenciées, réclame les financements promis par les pays développés et conteste les mesures commerciales unilatérales, notamment le mécanisme européen d'ajustement carbone aux frontières. Son expansion aux énergies renouvelables coexiste avec une forte dépendance au charbon. L'Inde prévoit pour 2035 une baisse de 47 % de l'intensité de ses émissions par rapport à 2005 et une part de 60 % de capacités électriques installées non fossiles. Son système électrique reste fortement dépendant du charbon. New Delhi défend la sécurité énergétique, le droit au développement et le financement international. À Belém, elle s'était opposée à toute mention explicite des combustibles. Le Brésil a défendu à Belém une feuille de route sur la sortie des énergies fossiles. Faute de consensus, cette proposition n'a pas été intégrée au texte final. La présidence brésilienne poursuit des travaux volontaires destinés à alimenter les discussions jusqu'à Antalya. L'Algérie entre intérêts gaziers et priorités africaines Grand fournisseur de gaz de l'Europe, membre du groupe arabe et pays exposé à la désertification, l'Algérie défend le gaz naturel comme ressource stratégique de la transition. Elle soutient également les renouvelables, la réduction du torchage et l'efficacité énergétique. Alger doit préserver ses recettes d'exportation tout en diversifiant son économie. Son appartenance au groupe arabe n'implique pas un alignement systématique sur les positions saoudiennes. À Antalya, elle devra concilier ses intérêts gaziers avec les priorités africaines : financement de l'adaptation, lutte contre la désertification et réponse au stress hydrique. Antalya, épreuve de crédibilité pour le multilatéralisme La COP 31 devra concilier des intérêts divergents. Les pays vulnérables réclament des financements prévisibles. Les partisans d'une réduction rapide des émissions veulent accélérer la sortie des combustibles fossiles. Les producteurs défendent leurs revenus et leur sécurité énergétique. Les pays en développement demandent un partage équitable des efforts. La présidence partagée entre Ankara et Canberra ajoute une difficulté institutionnelle. Le sommet sera jugé sur sa capacité à réduire les émissions, à mobiliser les financements annoncés et à renforcer l'adaptation. Antalya devra démontrer que le multilatéralisme climatique peut encore produire des décisions applicables malgré les rivalités géopolitiques, les divergences énergétiques et les inégalités de moyens. L’article COP 31 à Antalya, un test pour le multilatéralisme climatique : enjeux pour l’Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: India: End Crackdown on Protesters, Arbitrary Detentions
items.description: Click to expand Image Police detain protesters during a demonstration demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner, in New Delhi, India, October 10, 2026. © 2026 AP Photo/Manish Swarup (New York) – Indian authorities are using abusive methods to crack down on thousands of peaceful protesters in New Delhi and other Indian cities, Human Rights Watch said today. The protests, led by the Gen Z Cockroach Janta Party, opposition parties, student organizations, and civil society groups, have demanded the resignation of the country’s top election official over alleged wrongdoing and the scrapping of a contentious voter list revision process. As the protests grew in October 2026, the police have beat protesters, forcibly dragged them on the streets and stuffed them into vans and buses, arbitrarily detained them, imposed excessive restrictions on movement, and suspended mobile internet services. The authorities have also harassed and arbitrarily detained journalists covering the protests. “Police in Delhi are responding to peaceful protests with seemingly unnecessary or excessive force and have wrongfully detained thousands of people,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections.” Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration should stop the ill-treatment and arbitrary detention of protesters, allow people to protest peacefully, and restore mobile internet services and freedom of movement, Human Rights Watch said. Since June 2025, the Election Commission of India has carried out a nationwide Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to clean electoral rolls, ostensibly to remove any dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters. But the process, which has deleted more than 130 million names so far, has been arbitrary and opaque, prompting fears of mass disenfranchisement, and is disproportionately affecting Muslims and other religious minorities, women, and people living in poverty. Protest leaders and opposition parties allege that the commission has manipulated the lists to benefit Prime Minister Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The protests began on September 25, soon after the Indian Express published its investigation into alleged irregularities in the revision process. The newspaper found that the Election Commission’s two commissioners had raised multiple objections against decisions by the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Petitions challenging the revision process and seeking Kumar’s removal are before the Supreme Court. As protests in Delhi grew in October, security forces arbitrarily arrested and assaulted numerous protesters each day, and took them to undisclosed locations, later releasing many of them. Those detained included journalists and political opposition leaders, including four former chief ministers and Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition. When the protests began, Delhi Police released a set of “guidelines,” instructing journalists to “carry valid identity cards” that are “visibly displayed,” to “not obstruct police operations,” and to “maintain a reasonable and safe distance.” On October 11, the Supreme Court directed that lawyers and journalists “should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties.” On October 10 and 11, officials arbitrarily detained at least 30 journalists who were covering the protests. Four journalists’ organizations condemned the police actions, saying that journalists were “bundled into buses” used to detain protesters, and that police seized some of their phones and equipment. Three female journalists alleged that Delhi police officers sexually harassed them during the protests. A journalist from the magazine Caravan said that on October 11, police officers in Delhi hit him on the head several times, slapped him, and assaulted him with a rifle butt while he recorded them detaining a protester. “My press card was hanging by my neck but they still dragged me into the bus, ripping my shirt buttons,” a 31-year-old journalist told Human Rights Watch. Police detained him in a bus on October 10, and he was released only after the bus overheated and caught fire. “We could smell the fumes and had to shout at them to get us out,” he said. “The police personnel assaulted me and pinned me to the seat,” said John Brittas, a member of parliament participating in the protests, in a letter to the chief justice of India. The Cockroach Janta Party called for a protest on October 10 at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in Delhi. In response the authorities deployed over 40,000 security forces, canceled trains, shut down 43 metro stations, and suspended mobile internet services. Police took three Cockroach Janta Party leaders into custody aboard an airplane after it landed in Delhi, dragged several protesters from trains and buses who were traveling to Delhi, and put some youth leaders under house arrest. Air India has sought a response from the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security on how security forces entered its aircraft without prior authorization. On October 9, a police officer entered a Delhi mosque during Friday prayers to warn Muslims against participating in any “unnecessary protests.” The next day, police officials entered a Sikh temple in central Delhi to detain protesters who sought refuge there. Citizens for Fraternity-Bharat (CFF-Bharat), a civil society group that includes former government officials, has questioned why police entered religious premises and called for an independent inquiry. On October 11, India’s Supreme Court directed the authorities to ensure that people gathering peacefully are not illegally detained, internet services are restored, and people and traffic are allowed to move freely, subject to lawful restrictions. Thus far, the authorities appear to have ignored the directions. A journalist, 26, told Human Rights Watch he witnessed at least three instances in which BJP supporters and police chased protesters together. “It is collaborative,” said the journalist, who covered the protests on October 10. “The police looked on and did not stop the violence.” A female journalist, 27, said a group of about five men, some of them wearing saffron scarves, were beating protesters and targeting female journalists. “They were shouting at us, mocking us, and showing us the middle finger,” she said. “I saw two policemen laughing while the right-wing goons were kicking and beating protesters.” The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights expressed concerns over the mass detention of demonstrators and said that the government should engage in meaningful dialogue. The Indian Ministry of External Affairs called the statement “unwarranted” and “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India.” The Indian government should publicly direct security forces to respond to protests in accordance with international standards, notably the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials, Human Rights Watch said. “Indian authorities should allow people to protest peacefully by resuming transport services, removing unnecessary barricades, restoring the internet, and ensuring media freedom,” Pearson said. “Peaceful protest and freedom of expression are fundamental rights protected under the international human rights law that India’s leaders claim to uphold.”

items.title: Ghana signs UAE deal to create 5,000 overseas jobs
items.description: The government has signed an agreement with a United Arab Emirates (UAE) company to facilitate the recruitment of up to 5,000 Ghanaian workers for construction, building maintenance and facilities management jobs in Dubai. The Minister responsible for Labour, Jobs and Employment, Emmanuel Kwadwo Agyekum, signed the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Masa Depan Building Maintenance L.L.C., represented by its Managing Director, Junhong Deng. Recruitment will be carried out in phases, beginning with an initial batch of 500 workers, based on the company’s employment requirements. Under the agreement, the Ministry will coordinate recruitment in Ghana, verify job demands and employment contracts, facilitate skills testing and certification, and provide pre-departure orientation on UAE labour laws, workplace safety and workers’ rights. The arrangement is also intended to reduce irregular recruitment, prevent abuses involving recruitment fees and promote safe and orderly labour migration. Masa Depan Building Maintenance L.L.C. will directly employ the recruited workers and take responsibility for their wages, accommodation, insurance and other employer obligations. The company will also cover specified costs in the UAE, including visa and work permit fees, medical examinations, health insurance and air tickets from Ghana to the UAE. To safeguard the welfare of the workers, the agreement provides for occupational safety training, protective equipment, a worker welfare officer and a mechanism for submitting complaints without charge or retaliation. A Joint Working Committee will also monitor recruitment, employment conditions and the implementation of the agreement. The government says the partnership will expand access to international employment while strengthening protections against exploitation and unfair recruitment practices. It is also expected to support skills transfer and help returning workers reintegrate into Ghana’s labour market, with recruitment and deployment conducted in phases under the applicable labour laws of both countries.

items.title: UNDERSTANDING THE NEW AGE OF WAR
items.description: “And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?” *— William Butler Yeats, The Second Coming* OPENING NOTE William Butler Yeats’ chilling 1920 poem had a backdrop: World War I, the flu pandemic, the Russian Revolution and a sense of impending doom, an inflection point. The gyre is widening and turning again. As wars rage in Eastern Europe, the Middle East and West Asia, it is important to understand what’s happening and why. Questions abound. The answers are not easy to come by, given the unknowns. Here I intend to analyse how we have got here and what lies ahead. In the final section I also discuss how we theorise about war and why. Wars bring death and destruction. Technology helps. In our era, the pace of technological innovation (the Ukraine frontline is an example) has put Moore’s law on steroids. As the ongoing wars show, sequestering digital tech (like states did with nuclear weapons) and denying it to the adversaries is becoming increasingly difficult. Physical interconnectedness means the effects of war will spread beyond the spaces in which it is being fought; digital is non-spatial. Result: conflicts are creating ever more complex second- and third-order effects. War has become compounded. Commanders no longer stand on a knoll and cast Napoleon’s coup d’œil, the glance to judge the raging battle, and dispatch runners with new instructions. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and its cascading effects is a case in point, as are strikes by Ukraine on Russia’s oil refineries that, in conjunction with the war against Iran, have created an oil refineries crisis, forcing US President Donald Trump to ask Kyiv to go easy on those targets. Attacking Russia’s oil refineries is great targeting for Ukraine. Not so much for the rest of the world and energy markets. The war has also impacted US domestic politics and prices, not just the fuel price but also the bond market and its impact on mortgage payments. From the wars in Eastern Europe, the Middle East and West Asia and the changing balance between the United States, China and Russia, contemporary conflicts are becoming longer, more interconnected and harder to resolve. Theories that once helped us understand war struggle to keep up. Attrition, technological disruption, economic warfare and geopolitical rivalry are producing conflicts with no obvious finish line and an international system increasingly incapable of containing them Yet another problem is the finish line. X starts a war. Y fights back. Where in time and space does it end? Armies want decisive victories. Wars, increasingly, remain indecisive. Victory becomes contested. Iran against the US and Zionists; Ansar Allah against Saudi Arabia; Ukraine against Russia; the Taliban against Pakistan. This is not entirely new. Since World War II there have been many cases of tactical successes failing to achieve a war’s political objectives. That has now become a near-consistent menace for the stronger parties. Allied with it is what I call the ‘arena problem’, a direct outcome of compounding. The clash percolates into ether (information war, influence operations, cyber-attacks), financial and commodities markets, shipping and insurance (resulting in energy volatility, food insecurity, shortages of raw materials in petrochemical industries, the list is long). The kinetic embracing the non-kinetic in a new dialectic. The element of compounding and the absence of finish lines throw up another problem. War with its many battles is morphing into protracted conflicts that contain within them iterative wars and their battles, interspersed with pauses of uneasy, tenuous peace. As Nadia Schadlow, Trump’s former Deputy National Security Adviser for Strategy, has argued in a recent article for Foreign Affairs (‘America’s Attrition Trap’), belligerents increasingly have non-negotiable objectives. That leaves little room for compromise and makes conflicts intractable and wars within those conflicts attritional. Gone are the days of short, decisive wars when “relatively small numbers of sophisticated and expensive weapons systems” could devastate the enemy. Conflicts are now long and grinding. The world has learnt that the US does not have the industrial base that can rapidly replace many of the sophisticated munitions it has expended attacking Iran. Worse, it doesn’t have a strategy to create the political conditions required for victory. If attrition comes, can sustainment be far behind? No. Sustainment requires industrial assembly lines. The US won WWII because of its industrial output and innovation. It is now constrained by the inability to produce at scale. This isn’t a problem higher GDP can solve. As Schadlow notes, you can’t fire GDP from artillery tubes. That creates a gap “between nominal power and usable military capability.” When a war is happening, military theorists study it even as events are unfolding. While studying an ongoing war is crucial, it is important to remain wary of applying its lessons to every case. This is not to say that every war is absolutely different in its conduct. Just that one has to be careful in selecting what could apply to one’s own context. The Zionist war against Hamas and Hezbollah is not the same as a war against Iran or Ansar Allah. Sustainment and attrition are not new problems. The two great wars were all about attrition and sustainment. Attrition was taken for granted and it couldn’t be addressed without sustainment. Strategy incorporated both and industrial production responded to the challenge. That changed with the RMA (revolution in military affairs) in the 1980s. Lean became mean. Quality replaced mass in the field and scale on the factory floor. The wheel has turned again. But before we proceed, a word is in order about the environment in which the present threats are emerging. A Ukrainian soldier releases a drone near Bakhmut, Ukraine: drones already are and increasingly will be a ubiquitous menace, even in the hands of non-state actors | Reuters LIBERAL-INSTITUTIONALISM MAKES SHIP-WRECK When the Soviet Union passed into history, liberal institutionalism declared victory. US political scientist Francis Fukuyama told us history had ended though, in fairness, he had borrowed the term from the German philosopher Georg Hegel, who had meant it in a teleological sense, ie history had achieved its ultimate purpose. In his 2011 book, Canadian psychologist Steven Pinker came up with statistical abracadabra to tell us that violence had declined (Iraq and Afghanistan were happening). American political scientist Robert Keohane’s 1984 critique of hegemonic stability theory became the beacon for neoliberal policy. One-time US assistant secretary of defence Joseph Nye Jr gave us the soft power framework just before the demise of the Soviet Union. Power should attract and affect others to get the outcomes one wants. Culture and values played a crucial role, said Nye, as did foreign policy approaches that were grounded in legitimacy, cooperation and moral authority. Nye has passed on and is beyond these concerns now. Keohane is witnessing the unravelling but has dug in (that’s a separate debate). But the point is that there was much rejoicing all round. It seemed the party was over for the Realists. The Constructivists, a hybrid theoretical breed, were not to be left behind and found a backdoor to this victory ball. In any case, the long and the short of it was that, even without a world government, we were assured that we were close enough with the US as the benign unipole. Western and international institutions (the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, the European Union, the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation) were no longer just tools to manage the Cold War, they were the architecture of a new, rules-based, “liberal international order.” In an ideal world, perhaps — the hegemon establishing a just order and submitting to it before demanding that everyone else should too. Rules applying in equal measure to everyone. Except, the world got liberal hegemony. The hegemon sets the rules but wants to sit atop them, while coercing everyone else into submitting. That’s when the bondsman decides, in a Frantz Fanonian way, to fight back. That moment births consciousness, the value that asserts that there is a part of human nature, a baseline of human dignity and right, that none must be allowed to cross. Let’s now take a quick look at the current geopolitical scene before we round off with how we theorise about war. I eschew details because every item on the list can be written about at great length. BRAVE NEW WORLD John Mearsheimer marks 2017 as the end of the unipole anomaly. It’s not a random year but a structural pivot. Trump comes to power in the US and drops the language of the liberal international order. China’s economic miracle begins to translate into fast-paced acquisition of military capabilities. Putin’s two decades of efforts to resurrect and reassert Russia are succeeding and the US’ liberal hegemonic foreign policy now has rivals. International institutions and norms, never much comfort for the Global South, are unravelling, as are the legal standards and norms of international law (witness Trump’s recent tirade against the International Criminal Court). While many states, such as Japan, continue to support international institutions, they have to walk on eggshells, because the state that provides them security is the one taking its own edifice down brick by brick. The global state of affairs for arms control and non-proliferation is at its most dangerous and fragile point since the Cold War. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty between Russia and the US officially expired on February 5 this year without a successor agreement, which means there are no legally binding limits or mutual on-site inspections governing the strategic nuclear forces of the two. The 2026 Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference collapsed for a third time without achieving a consensus final document because of geopolitical gridlock. Meanwhile, the de facto global moratorium on nuclear explosive testing is under strain due to political rhetoric and modernisation efforts at test sites in the US, Russia and China (corollary: bilateral and multilateral nuclear guardrails are disappearing). The UN security council is paralysed and diplomacy is giving way to raw military coercion. Since Trump’s first term in office, sanctions and protectionism have weaponised trade, critical supply chains and international financial systems. That threatens the concept of a unified global economy. All of this is compounded by emerging tech (artificial intelligence or AI, robotics, lethal autonomous weapons). AI is already part of the kill chain while experts debate the moral, ethical and legal implications. Add to that hypersonic weapons as delivery systems, normalised rhetoric of nuclear brinkmanship (from Trump’s “a civilisation will be obliterated” to Putin’s threat on Kaliningrad) and the global architecture splitting into competing, militarised blocs, and we are watching the post-WWII order fray slowly and steadily. Result: escalating probability of global conflict and the return of Realist principles of anarchy and hard power. Which of course brings us back to war. WAR AND THEORIES Human consciousness is defined by a fundamental paradox. The inordinate desire and the ability to create surplus requires understanding our environment. But our environment, whether our immediate physical world, the cosmos, or human affairs, is rarely linear. Causality is not easy to understand, especially when dealing with human societies. To understand the complex non-linearity, the mind must simplify, slice and label things and events. Knowledge in this sense is reductive. We search for patterns and impose structures on the phenomena around us, to translate complexity into usable meaning. We build theories. There’s a slight problem, though. We want the theory to hold across time and space, to give us immutable principles and conquer temporality. It can’t, but we need boxes we can check. Theorising about war is no different. Readers are generally aware of such names as Carl von Clausewitz and Sun Tzu. But there are many more and no less important. All have written about war’s nature and its character. While there’s a general acceptance that war’s nature doesn’t change and it remains a violent clash of opposing political wills, the problem is structural. Three defining elements (and their sub-elements) form the basis of potential conflict. The first is anarchy, to be understood not as chaos but the absence of a central authority to which states can submit. This means that every state is ultimately responsible for its survival; it also means it has a security dilemma. By what means must it survive? Laws and institutions can help but they can’t ensure survival. The dilemma is that intentions can’t be predicted, so capabilities must be watched closely and matched. For instance, in a triadic situation such as Pakistan, India and China, Pakistan cannot assign a lesser value to its security simply because China could bail it out because of Beijing’s friction with New Delhi. Similarly, when India says that China is its primary threat and its military modernisation is to keep pace with China, Pakistan cannot rest easy because, in a conflict, India will not set aside certain capabilities as essentially China-specific and therefore unusable against Pakistan. The second element is power distribution. Its first sub-element is the return of more than one great power centre. In other words, the ‘tragedy’ of great power competition is back. The second element is the pressure generated by power transition. When the structural gap between a dominant superpower and a rising challenger narrows, the likelihood of inter-state conflict spikes. The third element is history’s persistent geopolitical flashpoints. We don’t arrive at any point with a clean slate. The past is etched on the slate. Geography becomes zero-sum: borders, sea-lanes, choke points, territorial claims, resource scarcity (water, for instance) and competition (oil/minerals). Resources are now entwined with tech competition and vulnerabilities: energy, water, rare earth minerals. With these elements taken as constants, we are left with the conduct of war. How to fight to win? Are there any principles involved? Can we figure out a non-spatial and non-temporal theory? In other words, can war be understood and even conducted on the basis of some theory across time and space? An Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy (IRGCN) speedboat approaches a cargo ship accused of violations in the Strait of Hormuz on April 21, 2026: the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and its cascading impact on the global economy exemplifies the changing nature of warfare | AFP CHANGING CONDUCT OF WAR Observing Napoleon keenly, Clausewitz insisted on total mobilisation and concentration of all forces towards crushing the enemy in battle. He even minimised the elements of surprise, deception and manoeuvre and believed that they might divert the commanders from advancing to battle as swiftly as possible. But he was in for a shock. After 20 years of developing his thought, he looked at France’s Spanish and Russian campaigns and realised that Napoleon’s adversaries had won against him by doing the opposite: avoiding battle, effecting deep withdrawals, using a scorched earth strategy, and, yes, guerrilla warfare. In fairness, Clausewitz wasn’t the only one looking at Napoleon. Antoine Jomini, his contemporary, observed Napoleon even more closely. In fact, Jomini’s entire theoretical framework was an attempt to codify Napoleon’s genius into a replicable science. Napoleon himself was deeply influenced by Comte de Guibert, whose 1772 work General Essay on Tactics argued for a highly mobile war of movement, independent combined-arms divisions and living off the land rather than relying on slow supply wagons. Napoleon essentially took Guibert’s theoretical concepts and executed them on the ground. Unfortunately for him, the damn Russians kept burning everything right up to Moscow and then burnt Moscow itself! Gen Giulio Douhet, the Italian air war strategist whose theories informed much of air war during World War II, argued that strategic airpower would be the decisive factor and conclude wars within hours or days. That hasn’t aged well, as we know from subsequent events and qualitative and quantitative analyses by various experts. Alfred Mahan was a US naval officer and naval war theorist. His ideas about securing maritime supply networks, controlling global sea choke points and projecting power through logistics remain fundamental to modern naval war and trade doctrine. The British, Germans and French studied him avidly. And yet, he thought of naval war like Douhet thought of air war. He lost focus on developments like the railways and the shifting balance between sea and land transportation. Surprisingly, he also thought little of commerce raiding and focused on the great naval battles. The German U-boats in WWII put paid to that. In fact, Churchill considered German commercial raiding the biggest threat in the Atlantic. It’s important to clarify that all these strategists distilled insightful ideas from actual wars. They were brilliant. In the case of Douhet, he understood the potential of war in the air, a new phenomenon. But the one flaw that underlay their theories was simple: they were looking for and tried to present a theory that was supposed to beat time and innovation. That’s generally a losing battle. Before WWI, military art looked at two levels: strategy studied war, while tactics looked at combat engagement. During the inter-war period, Russian theorists Aleksander Svechin and Georgii Isserson studied WWI, its immense scale, mass mobilisation and its wide geography. In his 1926 work Strategy, Svechin argued that a modern campaign is not a single clash, but a series of disjointed tactical engagements over wide geographies. War required an intermediate level. He called it operational art, the skill required by a commander to direct and chain these individual tactical battles together towards a unified strategic goal across time and space. He also recognised that wars would be attritive and require sustainment. Isserson turned the theoretical concept into practical methodology. In his influential 1936 book The Evolution of Operational Art, he laid out the blueprint for what he called Deep Battle — ie an offensive must strike the entire depth of the enemy’s deployment simultaneously. This was the seed that sprouted the concept of manoeuvre war. Germans were concurrently developing their manoeuvre doctrine (bewegungskrieg — movement warfare) under Gen Hans von Seeckt. They were focused on achieving a rapid, mobile outcome with highly capable forces, before an enemy could fully mobilise. Isserson was codifying a Soviet version of “distributed, manoeuvre-focused operations.” Both systems rejected the static linear gridlock of World War I in favour of dynamic, motorised movement. But here’s the thing. After the slaughter of infantry attacking lines in WWI, many argued that infantry had become passé. That was not to be. Tactical adjustments, fire and manoeuvre techniques, decentralisation of tactical command and mechanisation did not just keep infantry in play but it remains, to this day, the ultimate arbiter of victory, by holding and exploiting territory. Will it remain so, if and when robots and other lethal autonomous weapons are fielded, is unknown territory. A similar thing is happening to the tank in relation to the threat of direct attack and loitering munitions, as also tandem-charge anti-tank projectiles. The Falklands war began a debate about the usefulness of larger naval ships. They are still here and so will be the tank. Its armour protection relative to its weight and movement has reached an optimal level. The focus now is on local protection (defensive systems and tactics in the tank’s surrounding, to protect it from close-range and precision threats) through identifying and neutralising threats. As for the future, nothing is certain. I understand the desire to see into the future. But the point is simple: every theory must accept the limitations of time and space. Certain principles remain constant. Their application changes with technology. This is where we get into another trap. When a war is happening, military theorists study it even as events are unfolding. While studying an ongoing war is crucial, it is important to remain wary of applying its lessons to every case. This is not to say that every war is absolutely different in its conduct. Just that one has to be careful in selecting what could apply to one’s own context. The Zionist war against Hamas and Hezbollah is not the same as a war against Iran or Ansar Allah. The Russo-Ukraine war has two seemingly paradoxical trends: a static trenched frontline with conventional obstacles and another (with drones, counter-drones, satellite communications) where, to quote Schadlow again, the “feedback loop for learning [and innovation is running] directly from the battlefield to engineers and manufacturers and back again.” We are fighting against Afghanistan. That war and its conduct is very different from the wars we have fought against India and will likely fight in the future. Attrition and sustainment acquire relatively different meanings, for instance, in the case of India and Pakistan than they currently do in the case of Russia and Ukraine. Planning and execution, therefore, have to keep these subtle and more obvious differences in mind. Equally, certain developments will be shared across these different battlefields. Drones are one; missiles, another. On the defensive side, this means counter-drone tech (upgraded legacy anti-aircraft guns with radars and target-tracking sensors in close-in weapons systems against threats that have bypassed outer defensive layers) and anti-cruise and ballistic missile defences. Drones already are and increasingly will be a ubiquitous menace even in the hands of non-state actors. Commodification of tech means a lot of cheap but effective tech will be available to non-state actors through 3D-printing and information and instructions acquired from AI (Yemen’s Ansar Allah reportedly used Claude recently to hone target tracking and acquisition). Similar principles apply to force employment. For instance, Iran can afford to take defence in depth against ground incursions. Its land borders are sparsely populated and the terrain is formidable. It can allow an invading force to come in and give battle at a time and place of its choosing. Pakistan cannot. It lacks depth and the bulk of its urban infrastructure, lines of communication and population centres are in close proximity to Indian axes of advance. It has to ensure, in a contact war, to fight it on Indian soil. CLOSING THOUGHTS We need clarity. But clarity is very hard to come by. To offset the disadvantages of an approach that slices and dices, we introduced systems analysis and general systems thinking, borrowing the approach from biology, maths and engineering. It came as a decision-making tool to the Pentagon during the Cold War and seeped into the social sciences. The problem is that human systems are complex, reflexive and volitional and have a bad habit of undermining predictive models. Hegel and Marx introduced dialectics. Holistic knowledge in this sense is the ability to hold two opposing realities in mind simultaneously and trace how they shape each other over time. It sounds great but it too has limitations. Two opposing human forces is a game played by actors with free will, shifting emotions, and flawed information. In other words, dialectics can explain the nature of the struggle, but it cannot really map the outcome. That’s where we stand both in terms of the current trajectory of geopolitics as well as the outcome of that trajectory. The reason is simple: we are on a foggy slope and we don’t know where the precipice is. There are no real answers to the questions we have. Let no one tell you otherwise. The writer is a journalist interested in security and foreign policies. X: @ejazhaider Published in Dawn, EOS, October 11th, 2026

items.title: One Million Coders Programme targets 100,000 digital jobs in two years – Sam George
items.description: The government is targeting the creation of 100,000 digitally enabled jobs within the next two years under its flagship One Million Coders Programme, as it shifts its focus from digital skills training to employment opportunities. Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, said the new emphasis followed a directive from President John Dramani Mahama to ensure that beneficiaries of the programme could secure jobs after completing their training. Speaking during a monitoring visit to the Ashanti Region, he explained that while the National Democratic Congress’ manifesto committed to training one million Ghanaians in digital skills over four years, the government was also working to connect trained participants to businesses that need digital expertise. Mr George said the Ministry had presented the President with progress reports and remained confident of meeting the one-million training target within the administration’s four-year term. He said Ghana was seeking to build a large pool of skilled digital workers to meet growing demand for digital services, particularly from international companies looking to outsource work to the country. “We have shown His Excellency the trajectory the programme is on; we will cross a million in the four years. We are pivoting now away from the training into the job creation,” he said, expressing confidence in the employment target. He disclosed that the programme had already developed a pool of 10,000 data annotators whose skills could be presented to businesses seeking workers for specific digital assignments. The Minister’s visit to the Ashanti Region formed part of efforts to assess the programme’s progress and implementation at various training centres. He toured training centres and artificial intelligence laboratories at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology before visiting other facilities at Kwadaso, Asawase and Nkwantakese.

items.title: Bekwai MP inspects KNUST Medical School project, engages hospital management
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Bekwai, Ralph Poku-Adusei, has inspected progress on the KNUST Medical School project at the Bekwai Municipal Hospital as part of efforts to strengthen healthcare delivery and expand access to specialist services in the municipality. The visit, on Monday, October 12, 2026, also provided an opportunity for the MP to engage hospital management and staff on the facility’s achievements, ongoing projects and operational challenges following its accreditation by the Health Facilities Regulatory Agency (HeFRA) as a secondary-level health facility. Hospital management briefed Mr Poku-Adusei on the medical school project, which has received support from VALCO and is expected to position the facility as a teaching and training centre for future doctors. The project is also expected to improve access to specialist consultants for residents of Bekwai and surrounding communities. Addressing health professionals during the visit, Mr Poku-Adusei commended their dedication and sacrifices in advancing the hospital’s development. “Life is precious and good health is fundamental to everything we do. My commitment to supporting the welfare of my constituents transcends political differences,” he said. Medical Superintendent Dr Serebour and the management team outlined challenges confronting the hospital, including limited emergency unit capacity, the absence of a dedicated isolation unit, inadequate accommodation for critical health personnel, the lack of a CT scan facility and delays associated with laboratory equipment. Management also identified the need for infrastructure expansion and expressed interest in exploring public-private partnerships to establish a CT scan and advanced diagnostic centre. The MP pledged to provide free airtime on his FM platform to educate residents on hospital procedures, patient rights and health protocols. Management also briefed him on plans to introduce a queue management system to improve patient flow and reduce congestion and misunderstandings between patients and staff. Both parties agreed to maintain regular engagement towards developing the facility into a centre of excellence in the Ashanti Region.

items.title: NHIA seeks legal reforms to support Free Primary Healthcare
items.description: The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) is calling for amendments to the National Health Insurance Act, 2012 (Act 852), to accommodate the government’s Free Primary Healthcare initiative and population-based payment systems. Deputy Chief Executive Officer of the NHIA, Dr Kwesi Djokoto, told Parliament’s Health Committee that the existing legal framework needed to be updated to support the new healthcare financing arrangements and strengthen efforts to eliminate claims fraud, leakage and unauthorised charges imposed on patients. “The legal framework is something that has to be modified to accommodate the free primary healthcare and the population-based payment methods,” he said. Dr Djokoto said the Authority was pursuing tariff adjustments and deploying artificial intelligence (AI) and other digital tools to improve claims verification, identify fraudulent practices and address discrepancies between service tariffs and available funding for the National Health Insurance Scheme. He also highlighted plans to establish an anti-fraud and illegal payments directory to help prevent and detect unauthorised charges, including illegal co-payments, and ensure appropriate sanctions for offenders. He urged the committee to support the proposed legal changes, strengthen penalties for fraud and illegal co-payments, and help prioritise capital budget allocations for 2027. Dr Djokoto said the NHIA had already introduced electronic claims processing to improve efficiency and accelerate reimbursements to healthcare providers. “In summary, claims are fully electronic with 20 days turnaround time. We are paying monthly; we have digital interventions to enhance the work of the National Health Insurance Authority,” he said. President John Dramani Mahama launched the Free Primary Healthcare initiative on April 15, 2026, to provide essential first-contact medical services without charge at the point of use. Services are expected to be delivered through CHPS compounds, health centres, polyclinics, public health units, health posts, community pharmacies and mobile or container-based health kiosks in busy locations such as markets and lorry parks.

items.title: Beatrice Annan defends Afi Agbenyo’s EC appointment, cites record of gender advocacy
items.description: Presidential staffer Beatrice Annan has defended the appointment of Emelia Afi Agbenyo as Deputy Chairperson of the Electoral Commission (EC), arguing that her participation in political campaigns should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of partisan allegiance or a threat to electoral neutrality. Agbenyo’s appointment, alongside that of Dr Joseph Kweku Asamoah as another Deputy Chairperson, has drawn criticism from the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP). The party has questioned her suitability for the position, pointing to her involvement in the National Democratic Congress (NDC)’s campaign activities and her role as a spokesperson for its manifesto committee on governance. Her defenders, however, point to her professional experience in gender advocacy and policy work, including serving as a technical adviser and gender analyst with GIZ Ghana. Her involvement in the NDC’s 2020 and 2024 election campaigns has been explained as an effort to advance women’s representation in leadership rather than evidence of formal membership of the governing party. The defence also draws on her reported criticism of the NDC in 2016 over governance concerns and her warning before the 2024 elections that gender advocates could campaign against the party if it failed to retain a female running mate. These positions, her supporters argue, demonstrate that her engagement with political parties has been shaped by specific policy and gender-related issues. Speaking on Citi FM on Monday, October 12, 2026, Ms Annan insisted that Agbenyo had never been a card-bearing NDC member and had not demonstrated any conduct suggesting she would be biased in the performance of her duties. “She has not done anything to demonstrate any potential bias or imminent bias,” she said. She also maintained that the presidency followed the constitutional procedure for the appointments, explaining that the nominees were presented to the Council of State more than a month before their swearing-in and that the council undertook consultations with relevant stakeholders.

items.title: Ghana seeks investment deals in Bangkok amid global economic crises
items.description: Ghana is seeking investment and financing deals to advance its New Economy agenda at the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) in Bangkok, Thailand. The delegation, led by Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Baah Forson and supported by Bank of Ghana Governor Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, is engaging international investors, financial institutions and development partners on the sidelines of the meetings. The meetings, taking place from October 12 to 18 at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Centre, bring together representatives of the IMF’s 191 member countries and the WBG’s 189 members to deliberate global challenges involving debt, energy security, climate change among others. The rapid expansion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the economic impact of the US-Iran war are also on the agenda. For Ghana, the gathering offers an opportunity to mobilise investment ahead of the 2027 Budget, in which Dr Forson is expected to outline the Government’s New Economy agenda, its blueprint for the next phase of economic development. The agenda seeks to translate recent economic stabilisation into sustained transformation through value addition, industrialisation and improved global competitiveness, while creating jobs. Following the September IMF staff-level engagement in Ghana and the country’s exit from the US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility (ECF) programme, the Bangkok meetings are expected to advance discussions on benchmarks and reforms under the new Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI). Dr Forson is expected to engage IMF leadership, senior World Bank officials, finance ministers, representatives of international financial institutions and other development partners. He mentioned the shift towards the New Economy during the presentation of the 2026 Mid-Year Fiscal Policy Review. The 2027 Budget is expected to provide further details on how the Government intends to translate its development ambitions into policies and action. “Stabilisation was never the destination. It was the price of entry,” he stated. “Ghana has paid that price. What comes next is the work that changes lives at scale – the work of transformation.” At the 132 nd Monetary Policy Committee press briefing in Accra last month, Dr Asiama said Ghana would use the meetings to engage investors and development partners and secure beneficial agreements for the country. Responding to a question from the Ghana News Agency, he described the gathering as an important platform for bilateral engagements, allowing Ghana to present its economic programme directly to investors and development partners. “The annual meetings is where we get to meet our counterparts from the other side and to discuss Ghana’s economic programme… it is really an important meeting that all countries and officials do attend,” he said. Dr Asiama said the Ministry of Finance team would intensify investor outreach in Thailand to reassure markets and attract investment into key sectors of the economy. He expressed optimism that the engagements would yield positive results for Ghana. Globally, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva has warned of opposing forces shaping the economic outlook, with energy supply disruptions weighing on growth while AI-related investment supports demand. In her address ahead of the meetings, she said the IMF’s World Economic Outlook projected global growth at three per cent, with conflict-affected economies and vulnerable energy-importing countries facing significant pressures. She cited the continuing Russia-Ukraine war and the conflict in the Gulf as sources of uncertainty for the global economy. “Putting all of it together, my message to the world’s economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said. World Bank Group President Ajay Banga has said the global economy had remained resilient, supported by substantial AI investment and adjustments in oil supply. However, developing countries faced sharp increases in diesel and fertiliser costs, alongside risks associated with the El Niño weather phenomenon. He said the Bank was in active discussions with between 30 and 40 countries on possible crisis assistance to help them manage energy shocks, rising prices and the effects of the conflict in the Middle East. Mr Banga also said the Bank was advancing 14 to 15 debt-for-development swaps and guarantee projects designed to convert high-cost legacy debt into lower-cost financing linked to health, education and water programmes. Previous efforts has involved countries including Angola, Côte d’Ivoire and Argentina. Thailand is hosting the meetings for the second time, having previously hosted them in 1991. The return highlights the region’s growing role in discussions on global economic and financial stability. The Annual Meetings bring together central bank governors, finance and development ministers, private sector executives, civil society representatives, academics and the media for a common agenda. They discuss the global economy, financial stability, poverty reduction, inclusive growth, employment, climate change, among others pertinent global issues. . Key activities include the plenary session, meetings of the Development Committee and the International Monetary and Financial Committee. There will be regional briefings, press conferences and specialised forums.

items.title: IMF raises Ghana’s 2026 growth forecast to 5.7%, sees inflation falling to 4.8%
items.description: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised Ghana’s economic growth forecast for 2026 to 5.7% and projected year-end inflation at 4.8%, despite global economic pressures and uncertainty. The growth forecast represents an increase of 1.1 percentage points from the 4.6% projected in April. The projections are contained in the IMF’s latest economic outlook report, released on the sidelines of the Annual IMF/World Bank Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. Joy Business understands that the upward revision reflects Ghana’s commitment to fiscal discipline, spending targeted at stimulating growth, and strong commodity export earnings, particularly from gold. Higher gold export earnings have supported the country’s trade balance and helped build economic buffers. Ghana’s commitment to targets under the Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) programme also contributed to the revised outlook, according to information available to Joy Business. However, sources close to the Fund have expressed concern about Ghana’s reliance on gold exports and urged the government to diversify its export earnings. The IMF expects growth to moderate to 5.2% in 2027. Its 2026 forecast exceeds the government’s estimate of 4.8% outlined in the 2026 Budget, indicating a more optimistic assessment of Ghana’s growth prospects. According to the Ghana Statistical Service, the economy expanded by 6.0% in the second quarter of 2026, bringing the first-half growth to 6.2%. Inflation outlook The IMF projects that Ghana will end 2026 with inflation of 4.8%, down from its April forecast of 7.9%. The revised projection is also below the government’s and the Bank of Ghana’s target band of 8% ± 2 percentage points. That band ranges from 6% to 10%. With September inflation at 5.2%, the IMF’s forecast suggests a further easing in price pressures by the end of the year. Bank of Ghana internal projections cited by Joy Business had anticipated an increase in inflation in September, while expecting the year-end rate to remain within the target band. If the IMF’s forecast materialises, Ghana would record single-digit year-end inflation for a second consecutive year, following a similar outcome in 2025. World Bank on Ghana’s growth and inflation estimates The World Bank, in its Africa economic update released in October 2026, maintained its growth forecast of 4.8% for Ghana, unchanged from April. It projects 4.9% growth in 2027. The Bank expects growth to be supported by the services sector, a recovery in oil and gas activity, and continued progress with structural and fiscal reforms under national programmes. It described economic activity in the second quarter of 2026 as robust, although growth moderated slightly, with real GDP expanding by 6.0% year-on-year. On the expenditure side, the Bank said growth was supported by strong domestic demand. Investment increased by 53.0%, while domestic demand rose by 11.2%, reflecting continued strength in private and public spending. Impact The IMF’s improved outlook could strengthen investor confidence in Ghana’s economy and support efforts to attract foreign direct investment and additional assistance from development partners. For investors, stronger growth and lower inflation could improve perceptions of economic stability and the prospects for returns. Ghana’s participation in the PCI programme could also provide further reassurance to development partners about the government’s commitment to fiscal discipline. The outlook comes alongside recent upgrades to Ghana’s credit ratings by Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. Together, these developments could improve Ghana’s borrowing conditions and potentially lower the cost of future financing, including any eventual return to the international capital market. Global economic outlook The IMF said global economic activity had remained resilient, with the technology upturn, existing buffers and economic adjustments helping to cushion the effects of geopolitical disruptions. Nevertheless, it projects global growth to slow to 3.1% in 2026, then recover to 3.4% in 2027. Global headline inflation is expected to rise to 4.7% in 2026, then ease to 4.1% in 2027. Energy-importing economies outside the technology value chain face the most challenging outlook. The Fund warned that the factors supporting resilience have limits, with growth risks tilted to the downside. Further escalation of conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence, renewed trade tensions and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken economic activity. Conversely, stronger investment in artificial intelligence, associated productivity gains, and a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions could support faster growth. The IMF also called for stronger fiscal frameworks to respond to disruptive shocks and rebuild room for policy action through revenue measures.

items.title: Drame familial au marché de Dangbo au Bénin : Il poignarde à mort sa sœur jumelle qui lui prenait en charge
items.description: Dans la matinée de ce lundi, le marché communal de Dangbo a été le théâtre d’une tragédie d’une extrême violence. Une commerçante a été mortellement poignardée à son propre étal par son frère jumeau, qu'elle avait pourtant pris en charge à sa sortie de prison pour faciliter sa réinsertion. Immobilisé par les riverains puis remis à la Police républicaine, le suspect est désormais en garde à vue dans le cadre d'une enquête judiciaire ouverte par le parquet. La frénésie habituelle du marché communal de Dangbo s'est soudainement muée en une scène d'effroi sous les yeux de commerçants et d'usagers pétrifiés. Venu attaquer sa victime par surprise et muni d'une arme blanche, l'agresseur s'en est pris violemment à sa propre sœur jumelle alors qu'elle se trouvait à son étal de travail. Touchée à plusieurs reprises, la commerçante a succombé à ses blessures sur les lieux de l'agression avant même l'arrivée des secours, plongeant toute la localité dans la stupeur. L'affaire prend une tournure particulièrement troublante au regard des liens qui unissaient la victime à son bourreau. Tout juste libéré d'un établissement pénitentiaire, le frère jumeau bénéficiait de la solidarité constante de sa sœur, qui s'était engagée à subvenir à ses besoins quotidiens afin d'accompagner sa réinsertion. Toutefois, la cohabitation au domicile familial s'était détériorée au cours des derniers jours, rythmée par des tensions quotidiennes. Le choix délibéré de l'agresseur de se rendre armé directement sur le lieu de travail de sa bienfaitrice oriente désormais les investigations vers un acte mûrement réfléchi. La réaction des témoins présents sur le marché a été immédiate : les riverains sont parvenus à maîtriser et immobiliser le suspect sur place avant de le remettre aux forces de l'ordre. Dépêchée sur les lieux, la Police républicaine a sécurisé le périmètre et procédé aux premières constatations d'usage. Placé en garde à vue, le mis en cause doit être présenté incessamment devant le Procureur de la République. Une enquête judiciaire est actuellement en cours pour déterminer avec précision la chaîne des événements ainsi que les mobiles exacts de ce drame qui deuil la commune de Dangbo. L’article Drame familial au marché de Dangbo au Bénin : Il poignarde à mort sa sœur jumelle qui lui prenait en charge est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Ablakwa urges Africans not to view immigrants as threat to national progress
items.description: The Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, has urged African countries to view immigrants as contributors to national development rather than threats to economic progress. He said African countries could manage migration through effective regulation while respecting free movement protocols and protecting the rights of travellers. Mr Ablakwa made the remarks during an interview on TV3 on Saturday, October 10, 2026, while reacting to renewed tensions in South Africa following developments surrounding an apex court decision on the rights of asylum seekers. “We should not see immigrants and people who travel using our free movement protocols as people who are detrimental to our national progress. They are not parasites,” he said. He argued that countries could establish arrangements that regulate migration without violating the rights of people who travel across borders. “We can have an arrangement where we have regulated migration, where the free movement protocols are respected, where the rights of all persons are not violated just because they are travellers,” he added. Describing himself as a perpetual optimist about Africa’s future, the Foreign Affairs Minister said he remained confident in the continent’s integration agenda. He reaffirmed his belief in the vision of Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, that African countries could unite politically to achieve economic emancipation. According to him, although the continent has overcome significant challenges associated with colonialism, imperialism and political subjugation, it must now intensify efforts to tackle poverty and economic underdevelopment. “We have won the battle against political subjugation, colonialism, imperialism. We now must win the war against poverty, the war against economic underdevelopment. And I believe that can be achieved,” he said.

items.title: Mahama Cares must fund treatment, not looting – Asogli chiefs
items.description: The Asogli State has welcomed the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF), popularly known as Mahama Cares, while calling for transparent and responsible management of its resources. Togbe Kasa III, speaking on behalf of the Agbogbomefia of the Asogli State, described the Fund as a laudable initiative that could bridge gaps in the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and improve access to specialised healthcare. He said the initiative offered hope to people struggling to afford essential medical treatment but cautioned against the misuse of its resources. “The Fund should not be created for people to go and loot and share, but to take care of the healthcare needs of the population,” he said. He made the remarks when the GMTF Administrator, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, paid a courtesy call on the chiefs of the Asogli State as part of the Fund’s Volta Regional sensitisation tour. Togbe Kasa III commended the Administrator and her team for involving traditional authorities in public education on the Fund’s mandate, describing the engagements as essential to building awareness and support. He expressed optimism that the Fund would complement the NHIS by improving access to specialised medical services, particularly for patients unable to afford treatment. He said its success should be measured by how effectively it improved access to care and eased the financial burden on families facing serious medical conditions. Ms Darko-Opoku thanked the chiefs for receiving the delegation and stressed the need to extend public education on the Fund to communities across the country. She explained that the sensitisation exercise sought to help Ghanaians understand the Fund’s purpose, the support it offered and how eligible patients could access its interventions. She said the Fund needed to take its message beyond institutions and directly into communities, particularly to people unaware of the specialised healthcare support available to them. Ms Darko-Opoku added that collaboration with traditional authorities and other community leaders was essential to reaching more people with accurate information. The courtesy call formed part of the GMTF’s Volta Regional sensitisation tour, which aims to strengthen stakeholder collaboration and raise awareness of its interventions. The Fund was established to support the prevention and treatment of non-communicable diseases, improve access to specialised medical care and strengthen the training of specialist health professionals.
